tamil:
எண்ணிய எண்ணியாங்கு எய்துப எண்ணியார்
திண்ணியர் ஆகப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
ENNiya eNNiyaangu eydhupa eNNiyaar
ThiNNiyar aagap peRin.
current_meaning: If people who make plans stay firm in carrying them out, they will get what they planned, and in just the way they planned it.
elementary: If you decide to learn to ride a bike and you keep practising every day, even after wobbling, you will ride just the way you imagined. Wishing is the start; sticking with it is what makes the wish come true.
university: The couplet plays on eṇṇu (to think, plan) four times: eṇṇiya (what was planned), eṇṇiyāṅku (as it was planned), eṇṇiyār (those who planned), set against tiṇṇiyar (the firm), which chimes with tiṭpam in the chapter title. Parimelazhagar reads it as a promise conditional on firmness in execution: planners who are also firm doers obtain both the object and the manner they intended; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow him. On the text: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print eytu (எய்து), but the sandhi-joined edition at thirukkural-thamizh.org has eytupa (எய்துப, ‘they will attain’, future plural), and thirukkural.net’s own musical setting of the couplet by P. A. Muthukrishnan also quotes எய்துப; that reading, which the metre and grammar need, is adopted here. The couplet is one of the most often quoted in the Porul section, as a maxim that resolve turns intention into result.

tamil:
உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை வேண்டும் உருள்பெருந்தேர்க்கு
அச்சாணி அன்னார் உடைத்து.
transliteration:
UruvukaNdu eLLaamai vaeNdum uruLperundhaerkku
AchchaaNi annaar udaiththu.
current_meaning: Never look down on someone because of how small or plain they look. Some people are like the tiny pin that holds the wheel on a huge rolling chariot.
elementary: A giant temple chariot has huge wheels, but a tiny metal pin keeps each wheel from falling off. Without that little pin, the whole chariot stops! Some people are small or quiet, but they hold everything together, so never laugh at someone for being small.
university: Uru (form, size, appearance) and eḷḷāmai (not despising) open the couplet, and its image is the accāṇi, the small pin driven through the end of the axle (accu) that keeps the wheel of a great rolling temple chariot (uruḷ perun tēr) in place. Parimelazhagar, and Solomon Pappaiah after him, apply it within the chapter’s theme: men of firm mind may be small in body yet great in achievement, so they must not be judged by appearance; Kalaignar and Mu. Varadarasanar give it the wider moral that no one should be belittled for their size. The couplet reverses the usual link between bulk and strength, placing strength once again in firmness rather than outward form, as in 661. The three sources agree on the text; in sandhi form the lines read uruvukaṇ ṭeḷḷāmai vēṇṭu muruḷperuntērk / kaccāṇi yaṉṉā ruṭaittu.

tamil:
கலங்காது கண்ட வினைக்கண் துளங்காது
தூக்கங் கடிந்து செயல்.
transliteration:
Kalangaadhu kaNda vinaikkaN thuLangaadhu
ThookkanG kadindhu seyal.
current_meaning: Once you have clearly decided what to do, do it without wavering and without delay.
elementary: When you and your friends decide to build a treehouse, first think carefully. But once you’ve decided, don’t keep changing your mind or saying “maybe tomorrow.” Grab the hammer and start building!
university: The couplet moves in three steps: kalaṅkātu kaṇṭa vinai, an undertaking seen or decided without confusion (kalaṅku, to be muddied or agitated); tuḷaṅkātu, without wavering (tuḷaṅku, to tremble or sway); and tūkkam kaṭintu, having cast off tūkkam. Parimelazhagar takes tūkkam here as procrastination or delay (nīṭṭittal), not literal sleep, and the modern commentators follow him (Pappaiah: ‘without faltering and without delay’); Pope’s ‘mind unslumbering’ keeps the literal sense. The logic is that deliberation belongs before the decision, and firmness after it, which echoes the rule about deliberating and then acting in terintu ceyal vakai (ch. 47). The sandhi text reads viṉaikkaṭ ṭuḷaṅkātu, the same words written with the sandhi applied.

tamil:
துன்பம் உறவரினும் செய்க துணிவாற்றி
இன்பம் பயக்கும் வினை.
transliteration:
Thunpam uRavarinum seyka thuNivaatri
Inpam payakkum vinai.
current_meaning: Even if a lot of hardship comes your way, keep going bravely with work that will bring happiness in the end.
elementary: Learning to swim can be scary: water gets in your nose and your arms get tired. But if you keep going, one day you’ll zoom across the pool and love it. Some good things feel hard at first and happy at the end, so keep being brave.
university: The couplet sets tuṉpam (suffering) against iṉpam (joy), with the concessive uṟa variṉum, ‘even if it comes in abundance’ (uṟa, intensely), and the command ceyka tuṇivu āṟṟi, ‘act, sustaining courage’. Parimelazhagar explains that the suffering belongs to the beginning or the course of the undertaking while the joy is its fruit at the end, so a firm mind must not judge a task by its first taste; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah add ‘in the end’ (muṭivil) to make this explicit. Kalaignar reverses the emphasis, defining a joy-bringing act as one carried through despite suffering. The couplet sets up the chapter’s conclusion in 670. The three sources agree on the text.

tamil:
எனைத்திட்பம் எய்தியக் கண்ணும் வினைத்திட்பம்
வேண்டாரை வேண்டாது உலகு.
transliteration:
Enaiththitpam eydhiyak kaNNum vinaiththitpam
VaeNdaarai vaeNdaadhu ulagu.
current_meaning: No matter what other strengths they have, the world does not value people who do not value being firm in action.
elementary: A kid might be the fastest runner, the best drawer and the funniest in class, but if they never finish their part of the group project, nobody wants them on the team. Finishing what you start matters more than all the other talents.
university: The final couplet closes the chapter in a ring: eṉai-t-tiṭpam (firmness of whatever kind) echoes vinai-t-tiṭpam, and the line turns on the repeated vēṇṭu (to want, to value): vēṇṭārai vēṇṭātu, ‘does not want those who do not want’ firmness of action. Parimelazhagar takes eṉai-t-tiṭpam to mean the other strengths listed under 661 (wealth, army, allies and the like), and ulaku (the world) to mean the wise or great, who alone set a proper value on things; Solomon Pappaiah follows this with uyarntōr (the eminent), while Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep ‘the world’ at large. The effect is to restate 661 as a judgement of worth: firmness in action outranks every other kind of strength. The three sources agree on the text.

tamil:
சூழ்ச்சி முடிவு துணிவெய்தல் அத்துணிவு
தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது.
transliteration:
Soozhchi mudivu thunivu eydhal aththunivu
Thaazhchiyul thangudhal theedhu.
current_meaning: The goal of thinking things over is to reach a firm decision. Once you have decided, letting that decision sit and wait is harmful.
elementary: Imagine your team spends all of recess deciding which game to play, finally agrees on tag, and then just stands around until the bell rings. All that planning was wasted. This kural says: think carefully, decide, and then actually start.
university: The chapter opens by linking it to the preceding chapters on counsel (soozhchi, deliberation) and firmness in action (vinaith thitpam, ch. 67): the telos (mudivu) of counsel is thunivu, a settled resolve, not endless discussion. Thaazhchi means lowering, lagging or delay, and thangudhal 'to remain, to linger', so the second line pictures a resolve that has sunk into procrastination; theedhu (evil, harm) ranks such delay as a positive fault rather than mere inefficiency. Parimelazhagar glosses the kural as teaching that once the ministers' counsel has concluded in a decision, the king must not let time pass before execution, because delay lets circumstances and the enemy change. Older editions print the couplet with full sandhi (துணிவெய்த லத்துணிவு / தாழ்ச்சியுட் டங்குத றீது), as in thirukkural-thamizh.org, but the words are identical. The maxim closely matches the proverb Aristotle cites in Nicomachean Ethics VI.9: deliberate slowly, execute quickly.

tamil:
தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால தூங்கற்க
தூங்காது செய்யும் வினை.
transliteration:
Thoonguga thoongich cheyarpaala thoongarka
Thoongaadhu seyyum vinai.
current_meaning: Take your time with tasks that should be done slowly. But never delay tasks that must be done right away.
elementary: Planting a tree is something you can take your time over, choosing the best spot. But if the bathtub is overflowing, you turn off the tap right now. A wise person knows which jobs can wait and which cannot.
university: The couplet is a famous piece of verbal play: the verb thoongu appears five times, in the sense of 'to delay, to be slow, to tarry' (literally to droop or hang, and by extension to sleep). Parimelazhagar explains that some undertakings (such as those whose moment has not yet come) are properly done by waiting, while others (such as those where the opportunity or the enemy will not wait) must be done without any delay; the skill lies in telling the two apart. The kural therefore qualifies 671: the rule is not simply 'hurry' but correct timing, echoing the earlier chapter on knowing the right time (kaalam aridhal, ch. 49). Modern commentators Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it the same way, and there are no significant textual variants. It pairs naturally with the Latin-Greek motto festina lente and with Francis Bacon's essay on delays.

tamil:
ஒல்லும்வா யெல்லாம் வினைநன்றே ஒல்லாக்கால்
செல்லும்வாய் நோக்கிச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Ollumvaai ellaam vinai nandre ollaakkaal
Sellumvaai nokkich cheyal.
current_meaning: Whenever you can act directly, that is best. When you cannot, find another way that will work and do it that way.
elementary: If the front door is open, you walk straight in. If it is locked, you don't give up; you go round to the back door or ask someone for the key. Pick the way that actually works.
university: Ollum vaai means 'where it is possible (feasible)', and sellum vaai 'the way that will go through, the effective route'. Parimelazhagar reads vinai here in its political sense of open action against an enemy, that is, danda (force), the last of the four classical expedients (sama, dana, bheda, danda); where force can succeed it is best, and where it cannot one must choose among the remaining expedients. Solomon Pappaiah follows this reading explicitly, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the couplet more generally as 'do the work directly where you can, otherwise find a workable way'. The older sandhi text reads வினைநன்றே யொல்லாக்காற் with no difference of meaning. The teaching is pragmatic flexibility of means within a fixed end, a theme shared with the Arthashastra and later Machiavelli.

tamil:
வினைபகை என்றிரண்டின் எச்சம் நினையுங்கால்
தீயெச்சம் போலத் தெறும்.
transliteration:
Vinai pagai endru irandin echcham ninaiyungaal
Theeyechcham polath therum.
current_meaning: Think about it: an unfinished task and an enemy not fully beaten are like leftover sparks of a fire. They can grow back and destroy you.
elementary: When you put out a campfire, you pour water until every last glowing coal is out, because one hidden ember can start a big fire later. A job left half-done, or a quarrel only half-settled, is like that ember.
university: Echcham means 'remainder, leftover', and theeyechcham 'the remnant of a fire'; therum means 'will burn, will destroy'. Parimelazhagar notes that an unfinished undertaking and a partly subdued enemy both look small and harmless, but grow unnoticed, like smouldering embers, until they destroy the one who neglected them; Mu. Varadarasanar stresses this unseen growth. The thought is a commonplace of Indian niti: the Mahabharata's counsel of Kanika (Shanti Parva 12.138.58, critical edition) lists the remnant of a debt, of a fire and of an enemy as things that grow again and again if left unchecked. The older sandhi text reads வினைபகை யென்றிரண்டி னெச்ச நினையுங்காற் / றீயெச்சம் with no change in meaning. Modern readers often apply the enemy half to unresolved conflicts or problems rather than literal foes.

tamil:
பொருள்கருவி காலம் வினையிடனொடு ஐந்தும்
இருள்தீர எண்ணிச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Porul karuvi kaalam vinai idanodu aindhum
Irul theera ennich cheyal.
current_meaning: Before you act, think clearly about five things until nothing is unclear: money, tools, timing, the task itself, and the place.
elementary: Before baking a cake you check: Do I have the ingredients? Do I have a bowl and an oven? Do I have enough time before dinner? Do I know the recipe? Is the kitchen free? Once all five are clear, you start.
university: The kural lists five factors: porul (wealth, resources), karuvi (instruments, which Parimelazhagar extends to the army and other means), kaalam (time), vinai (the nature and method of the act itself) and idam (place). Irul theera, 'until the darkness is dispelled', means until every doubt has been removed. Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah add that each factor must be weighed for both oneself and the enemy, so this is a comparative strategic appraisal and not just a checklist. The structure closely matches the Arthashastra's five limbs of counsel (1.15), which include means, men and materials, and the apportionment of place and time, and it summarises earlier Kural chapters on strength (48), time (49) and place (50). Older editions print the line with full sandhi (வினையிடனொ டைந்து / மிருடீர வெண்ணிச் செயல்).

tamil:
முடிவும் இடையூறும் முற்றியாங்கு எய்தும்
படுபயனும் பார்த்துச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Mudivum idaiyoorum mutriyaangu eydhum
Padupayanum paarththuch cheyal.
current_meaning: Act only after looking at what it takes to finish the task, the problems that may come up along the way, and the gain it will bring at the end.
elementary: Before starting a big jigsaw puzzle, ask: How long will it take to finish? What could go wrong, like the cat scattering pieces? And will the finished picture be worth it? If yes, begin.
university: Mudivu here is read by Parimelazhagar as the effort (muyarchi) required to bring the work to completion, idaiyooru as the hindrances that may come in between, and padupayan as the large yield obtained when it is completed (mutriyaangu eydhum). The kural thus sets out a three-part cost-benefit appraisal: cost of completion, risk, and return. Mu. Varadarasanar reads mudivu more simply as 'the way of completing the task', while Kalaignar reorders the three items but keeps the sense. The older sandhi text reads முடிவு மிடையூறு முற்றியாங் கெய்தும், with no difference of meaning. The idea anticipates the Gospel image of counting the cost before building, and Epictetus' advice to consider what comes before and after any undertaking.

tamil:
செய்வினை செய்வான் செயன்முறை அவ்வினை
உள்ளறிவான் உள்ளம் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Seyvinai seyvaan seyanmurai avvinai
Ullarivaan ullam kolal.
current_meaning: The right way to do a task is to find out what someone who knows that task well thinks about it.
elementary: If you want to learn to bake bread, the best first step is to ask a baker who has done it a thousand times. They know the little secrets no recipe tells you.
university: Ullarivaan means 'one who knows the inside' of the work: its hidden difficulties, tricks and secrets. Ullam kolal means 'to take (on) his mind or view'. Parimelazhagar glosses the knower as someone who has already carried out such an undertaking and knows its secret (marmam), and Solomon Pappaiah likewise reads 'one who has done this work before'. The sound pattern (seyvinai seyvaan seyanmurai; ullarivaan ullam) is deliberate and makes the couplet easy to remember. The older sandhi text reads செயன்முறை யவ்வினை / யுள்ளறிவா னுள்ளங் கொளல். The kural extends the earlier chapter on seeking the help of the great (periyaaraith thunaikkodal, ch. 45) to the practical level of expertise.

tamil:
வினையான் வினையாக்கிக் கோடல் நனைகவுள்
யானையால் யானையாத் தற்று.
transliteration:
Vinaiyaan vinaiyaakkik kodal nanaikavul
Yaanaiyaal yaanaiyaath thatru.
current_meaning: Using one task to get another one done is like using a trained elephant to catch a wild one.
elementary: When you go to the shop to buy milk and also post a letter on the way, one trip does two jobs. Long ago, people caught wild elephants by using a tame elephant to lead them in. Smart people let one job help with the next.
university: Nanaikavul, literally 'wet cheek', refers to an elephant in musth, whose temples stream with fluid; such tame elephants were used as decoys to lure and capture wild ones, a practice well attested in Tamil and Sanskrit sources on elephant-keeping. Vinaiyaan vinai aakkik kodal means 'to bring about a (further) task by means of a task'. Parimelazhagar specifies that the second undertaking should be of the same kind as the first, just as elephant catches elephant, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as completing one task while doing another. The older sandhi text reads கோட னனைகவுள் / யானையால் யானையாத் தற்று. The elephant simile gives a vivid image of turning one achievement into the means of the next.

tamil:
நட்டார்க்கு நல்ல செயலின் விரைந்ததே
ஒட்டாரை ஒட்டிக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Nattaarkku nalla seyalin viraindhadhe
Ottaarai ottik kolal.
current_meaning: Winning over people who are not yet on your side is more urgent than doing good things for people who are already your friends.
elementary: Your friends already like you. But if there is a kid in class who keeps fighting with you, making peace with them first can make everything easier for everyone. Turning a rival into a friend is the urgent job.
university: Nattaar are those already bound in friendship; ottaar are those who do not adhere to one, that is, rivals or foes, and ottik kolal is 'to make them adhere, to bring them round'. Parimelazhagar, followed by the Drew-Lazarus translation reproduced on ytamizh, specifies the foes of one's foes, so that the kural advises quickly securing allies against a common enemy before an undertaking, while modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) read it more broadly as reconciling enemies. Viraindhadhu, 'the more urgent', ranks this ahead of kindness to friends because friends are already secure while potential enemies can still change sides. The older sandhi text reads விரைந்ததே / யொட்டாரை யொட்டிக் கொளல். The kural fits the Indian mandala theory of alliances and also anticipates ethical teachings about turning an enemy into a friend.

tamil:
உறைசிறியார் உள்நடுங்கல் அஞ்சிக் குறைபெறின்
கொள்வர் பெரியார்ப் பணிந்து.
transliteration:
Uraisiriyaar ulnadungal anjik kuraiperin
Kolvar periyaarp panindhu.
current_meaning: Leaders of a small country, afraid that their own people are scared, will give in to a stronger power and accept peace if they are offered a chance.
elementary: Imagine a small team facing a much bigger, stronger team and all your players are scared. A wise captain might agree to a fair deal instead of a hopeless match, to protect the team. Sometimes the brave choice is to make peace.
university: Uraisiriyaar, 'those whose dwelling (realm) is small', is read by Parimelazhagar as the ministers of weak states; ulnadungal anji means 'fearing the inner trembling' of their own subjects; kurai perin, 'if they obtain an opening' for reconciliation; periyaarp panindhu kolvar, 'they will submit to and embrace the great'. The Drew-Lazarus rendering on ytamizh follows this reading, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it more generally about the weak yielding to the strong for the sake of their people. The older sandhi text reads உண்ணடுங்க லஞ்சிக் குறைபெறிற். Placed at the end of the chapter, the kural completes the method of execution by admitting that sometimes the wise act is timely submission rather than conflict, a principle also central to the Arthashastra's teaching on the weak king and to Luke 14:31-32.

tamil:
அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல் வேந்தவாம்
பண்புடைமை தூதுரைப்பான் பண்பு.
transliteration:
Anbudaimai aandra kudippiraththal vendhavaam
Panbudaimai thoodhuraippaan panbu.
current_meaning: An envoy (a messenger sent to speak for a king) should be loving, come from a respected family, and have the good manners that kings value.
elementary: When your class sends someone to ask the principal for a longer break, you pick a kind person who comes from a family everyone trusts and who knows how to be polite to grown-ups. The person carrying a message has to be someone the listener already respects.
university: The chapter on the envoy (tūtu) belongs to the Amaichiyal, the section on ministers (chs. 64-73), and opens with the general qualifications. Parimelazhagar glosses aṉpuṭaimai as affection toward one’s own kin (cuṟṟattār), ‘āṉṟa kuṭi’ as a family fit to bear ministerial office, and ‘vēntu avām paṇpu’ as the qualities royalty desires. He adds that kin-affection means the envoy keeps his relatives from harm, and good lineage means he has heard of envoy-craft from his forebears. Manakkudavar reads the first quality differently, as love for one’s own king, and explains ‘qualities kings desire’ as not coveting what the king covets. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar keep the three-part list, Pappaiah widening the love to people, state and kin. On the text: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற; the sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh.org reads அன்புடைமை யான்ற, the same words with the glide written in.

tamil:
அன்பறிவு ஆராய்ந்த சொல்வன்மை தூதுரைப்பார்க்கு
இன்றி யமையாத மூன்று.
transliteration:
Anbarivu aaraaindha solvanmai thoodhuraippaarkku
Indri yamaiyaadha moondru.
current_meaning: Love for the king, knowing what is good for him, and the skill of choosing the right words are three things an envoy must have.
elementary: Imagine you are sent to ask the neighbours to give back your family’s ball. You need three things. You have to care about your family, you have to know exactly what to ask for, and you have to pick your words well so the neighbours say yes.
university: The couplet names three indispensable (iṉṟiyamaiyāta) qualities. Parimelazhagar makes each one specific: aṉpu is love for one’s own king, aṟivu is knowing what is good for him, and ārāynta colvaṉmai is careful speech before foreign kings. He explains the ‘examining’ (ārāytal) as choosing words the other side will agree to. From ‘indispensable three’ he infers that the ministerial virtues listed earlier are also needed. He also notes that 681 and 682 give the general marks common to both kinds of envoy the chapter goes on to separate. Solomon Pappaiah reads aṉpu as love of country, and Kalaignar gives a plain list. The couplet looks back to chapter 65 (Colvaṉmai, power of speech). On the text: the sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh.org runs the words together (அன்பறி வாராய்ந்த … தூதுரைப்பார்க் கின்றி யமையாத), with no change of wording.

tamil:
நூலாருள் நூல்வல்லன் ஆகுதல் வேலாருள்
வென்றி வினையுரைப்பான் பண்பு.
transliteration:
Noolaarul noolvallan aagudhal velaarul
Vendri vinaiyuraippaan panbu.
current_meaning: A person who goes before kings with spears to speak for their own king's success must be the most skilled scholar even among the learned.
elementary: If you have to explain your team’s plan to the biggest, toughest team in the playground, you had better know the rules of the game better than anyone there. Knowing more than the clever people is what keeps you safe in front of the strong ones.
university: The couplet contrasts two audiences: nūlār, those learned in the treatises, and vēlār, the spear-bearers. Parimelazhagar identifies the first as the foreign court’s ministers, learned in nīti-nūl (works on polity), and the second as foreign kings. He says Valluvar wrote ‘vēlār’ to evoke their readiness to kill (kōṟal mālaiyar), and ‘veṉṟi viṉai’ to cover both kinds of envoy’s work. To be ‘vallaṉ’ (master) is more than knowing the texts: it is being able to set them out and apply them in front of ministers who only know them. Manakkudavar reads nūlāruḷ nūlvallaṉ as being able to expound all the texts before the learned. Pappaiah stresses knowledge of political ethics in a hostile court. On the text: the sandhi-joined text reads நூலாரு ணூல்வல்ல னாகுதல், the same words as the split form (நூலாருள் நூல்வல்லன் ஆகுதல்) in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அறிவுரு வாராய்ந்த கல்விஇம் மூன்றன்
செறிவுடையான் செல்க வினைக்கு.
transliteration:
Arivuru vaaraaindha kalvi-im moondran
Serivudaiyaan selga vinaikku.
current_meaning: Send a person on the mission only if they have three things together: good sense, a fine appearance, and learning that has been tested.
elementary: To show the new kid around school, the teacher picks someone who is smart, looks neat and friendly, and has learned the school rules properly. Someone with only one of these would not be enough. You need all three together.
university: Parimelazhagar makes each of the three precise. Aṟivu is innate intelligence (iyaṟkai aṟivu). Uru is a presence that viewers find attractive (kaṇṭār virumpum tōṟṟap polivu). Ārāynta kalvi is learning that has been examined ‘with many, over a long time’. The key word is ceṟivu, ‘combination’ or ‘density’: he notes that the three rarely come together in one person, and that together they make the envoy respected, so the mission succeeds. ‘Viṉai’ is the business of embassy to foreign kings. Manakkudavar reads ceṟivu as ‘containment’ (aṭakkam). Pappaiah adds that the person should be able to frame his message himself, which anticipates the ‘self-composing’ envoy of 687. On the text: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print கல்விஇம் மூன்றன் (a vowel hiatus); the sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh.org reads கல்வியிம் மூன்றன், with the glide y written in.

tamil:
தொகச்சொல்லித் தூவாத நீக்கி நகச்சொல்லி
நன்றி பயப்பதாந் தூது.
transliteration:
Thogachchollith thoovaadha neekki nagachcholli
Nandri payappadhaan thoodhu.
current_meaning: A good envoy sums things up briefly, leaves out harsh words, speaks so pleasantly that people smile, and so brings good to their king.
elementary: If you need to tell a friend they broke your toy, you don’t list every bad thing they ever did. You say it short, you leave out the mean words, and you say it kindly, maybe with a smile. Then they are much more likely to help fix it.
university: Parimelazhagar reads the three verbs as two techniques. Tokac colli is condensing: when many demands must be made, state the one cause from which they all follow, so the other side agrees because the point is short and has to be worked out. Tūvāta nīkki naka colli applies to unwelcome demands: drop the harsh words (veyya col) and put things so pleasantly that the listener agrees without feeling the sting. Both serve naṉṟi payattal, securing benefit for one’s own king. Manakkudavar says the couplet teaches ‘how to speak’. Kalaignar glosses tūvāta as what would provoke anger, and Varadarasanar as what is useless. The couplet repeats the ideals of chapter 65 on speech, applied to diplomacy. On the text: all sources agree; the final தூது follows நன்றி பயப்பதாம் with the m assimilated (பயப்பதாந்).

tamil:
கற்றுக்கண் அஞ்சான் செலச்சொல்லிக் காலத்தால்
தக்கது அறிவதாம் தூது.
transliteration:
Katrukkan anjaan selachchollik kaalaththaal
Thakkadhu arivadhaam thoodhu.
current_meaning: A good envoy is well-learned, is not scared by angry looks, speaks so the message sinks in, and knows what is right for the moment.
elementary: Sometimes when you explain something important, the other person frowns at you. A brave messenger doesn’t run away or start stammering. They keep calm, say it clearly so it is understood, and think about what will work best right then.
university: Parimelazhagar rearranges the clauses: kaṟṟu (having studied the works on polity), cela colli (speaking so the enemy king takes the message to heart), kaṇ añcāṉ (not fearing his glare, ceyirttu nōkku), and kālattāl takkatu aṟivatu (knowing the means suited to the time). He explains why learning comes first: it teaches the means (upāyam), and if the moment calls for another method, the envoy must be able to change course. Manakkudavar gives kaṟṟu a narrower sense, having learned how to calm a foreign king who becomes angry. Pappaiah calls the timely skill a strategic path (tantira vazhi). ‘Kaṇ añcāṉ’ goes back to the Sangam ideal of the unflinching gaze (vaṉkaṇ), which returns in 689. On the text: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read காலத்தால் / தக்கது அறிவதாம்; the sandhi-joined text reads கற்றுக்கண் ணஞ்சான் … காலத்தாற் / றக்க தறிவதாந் தூது, the same wording.

tamil:
கடனறிந்து காலங் கருதி இடனறிந்து
எண்ணி உரைப்பான் தலை.
transliteration:
Kadanarindhu kaalang karudhi idanarindhu
Enni uraippaan thalai.
current_meaning: The best envoy knows their duty, waits for the right time, chooses the right place, and thinks carefully before speaking.
elementary: If you want to ask your parents for a puppy, the smartest way is to wait until they are relaxed, not in the middle of a busy morning. Pick a good spot, and practise what you will say and what they might answer. That is how the best messengers do it.
university: Parimelazhagar glosses kaṭaṉ as the proper conduct toward foreign kings, which comes from weighing their standing, one’s own king’s and one’s own. Kālam is their cevvi, the mood in which they are receptive. Iṭaṉ is a place where one’s supporters are at hand. Eṇṇi means rehearsing in advance one’s own words, the other side’s likely replies, and one’s counter-replies. He says Valluvar chose ‘talai’ (the foremost) because the Sanskrit treatises (vaṭanūlār) rank envoys as first, middle and last, the last being a mere letter-carrier. With this couplet ends the section (681-687) on the envoy who frames his own words (tāṉ vakuttuk kūṟuvāṉ). The following three couplets deal with the envoy who repeats a given message. Manakkudavar likewise calls this the mark of the foremost envoy. On the text: the sandhi-joined text reads கருதி யிடனறிந் / தெண்ணி யுரைப்பான் றலை, the same wording.

tamil:
தூய்மை துணைமை துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்றின்
வாய்மை வழியுரைப்பான் பண்பு.
transliteration:
Thooymai thunaimai thunivudaimai immoondrin
Vaaymai vazhiyuraippaan panbu.
current_meaning: A person who carries the king's message exactly as given must be honest and clean, have good helpers, be brave, and above all tell the truth.
elementary: When your teacher gives you a note for your parents, you shouldn’t swap the words for a treat, you should have a grown-up nearby who can help, you should be brave enough to deliver it even if it’s bad news, and you must never change what it says.
university: From here Parimelazhagar turns to the second kind of envoy, the vazhi uraippāṉ, who repeats his king’s words exactly as spoken. He gives each quality a job. Tūymai is purity from greed for wealth or women (poruḷ kāmaṅkaḷ), so bribes cannot bend the message. Tuṇaimai is having the foreign ministers’ support, so that if the envoy’s praise of his own king angers them, they can smooth it over by saying ‘that is how our people speak’. Tuṇivuṭaimai is boldness, so he does not hold back out of fear of harm. Vāymai is truthfulness, so everyone can trust him. He reads ‘immūṉṟiṉ’ with the -iṉ in the sense of ‘together with’: truthfulness is a fourth quality alongside the three. Manakkudavar differs: tuṇaimai is having kin, tuṇivu is resolving after inquiry. Pappaiah follows Parimelazhagar closely. On the text: all sources agree; the sandhi-joined text writes யிம்மூன்றின்.

tamil:
விடுமாற்றம் வேந்தர்க்கு உரைப்பான் வடுமாற்றம்
வாய்சேரா வன்க ணவன்.
transliteration:
Vidumaatram vendharkku uraippaan vadumaatram
Vaaysera vankanavan.
current_meaning: Only a person strong enough never to let a shameful word slip out should carry their king's message to other kings.
elementary: Suppose you are sent to tell a bigger kid that your friend wants his bike back. If the big kid scares you, it’s tempting to say ‘my friend is silly, never mind’. A good messenger stays strong and never says something that makes the person who sent him look bad.
university: Viṭu māṟṟam is ‘the word sent’, the king’s message. Vaṭu māṟṟam is ‘a word that scars’. Parimelazhagar explains this as words that lower one’s own king, which the envoy might say out of fear of harm to himself. Vaṉkaṇ is the firmness never to let such words out, even by a slip of the tongue (vāy cōrntum). He says ‘vaṭu’ (a scar) was chosen because such lowering goes against the duty of one’s station (cāti tarumam). He also notes that ‘vāy cērā’ expresses the result (not speaking) through its cause (firmness). Manakkudavar calls the quality añcāmai, fearlessness. Pappaiah and Kalaignar stress not saying anything wrong or demeaning when danger threatens. On the text: ytamizh.com prints the couplet without a final stop; thirukkural.net and the sandhi-joined text have வன்க ணவன். in the metrical division; thirukkuralvilakkam.blogspot.com joins it as வன்கணவன். Some editions give வாய்சோரா for வாய்சேரா (Parimelazhagar’s gloss uses ‘வாய்சோர்ந்தும்’), but the sources consulted read வாய்சேரா.

tamil:
இறுதி பயப்பினும் எஞ்சாது இறைவற்கு
உறுதி பயப்பதாம் தூது.
transliteration:
Irudhi payappinum enjaadhu iraivarku
Urudhi payappadhaam thoodhu.
current_meaning: A true envoy delivers the king's whole message and works for the king's good, holding nothing back, even if it costs the envoy their life.
elementary: Think of a lifeguard who swims out to someone in trouble even though the waves are scary. A true messenger is like that. Even when delivering the message is frightening or dangerous, they carry it all the way for the people who trusted them.
university: Iṟuti is ‘end’, meaning death. Eñcātu is ‘without leaving any of it out’. Uṟuti is ‘firm good’ or advantage. Parimelazhagar: even if the words will end the envoy’s life, he does not hold back out of fear, and he speaks his king’s position to foreign kings exactly as told. He adds that by naming death, the worst outcome, Valluvar leaves lesser dangers without need of mention. With 688-690 the chapter completes its account of the envoy who repeats a given message (kūṟiyatu kūṟuvāṉ). The couplet ends the chapter on its highest demand, loyalty to the death, and prepares for chapter 70 on conduct in the king’s presence. All modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) read iṟuti as the envoy’s own death. On the text: the sandhi-joined text reads பயப்பினு மெஞ்சா திறைவற் / குறுதி, the same wording as the split form.

tamil:
அகலாது அணுகாது தீக்காய்வார் போல்க
இகல்வேந்தர்ச் சேர்ந்தொழுகு வார்.
transliteration:
Akalaadhu anukaadhu theekkaaivaar polka
Ikalvendharch serndhozhuku vaar.
current_meaning: People who serve moody, powerful kings should act like people warming themselves by a fire. They should not go too far away or too close.
elementary: On a cold night you sit near a campfire. Too far away and you shiver; too close and you get burned. Being around a very powerful person is the same: stay close enough to be useful, but never so close that you get burned.
university: The chapter opens the Kural’s treatment of how the minister or courtier (the Amaichiyal section) is to conduct himself with the ruler, and its governing image is the fire (thee) at which one warms oneself (theekkaaivaar). The paired negatives akalaadhu (not withdrawing) and anukaadhu (not approaching) define a calibrated middle distance rather than a fixed rule. Parimelazhagar reads ikalvendhar as kings whose temper easily turns to hostility (ikal = enmity, variance), so the danger is not the king’s wickedness but his volatility: the same fire that warms can burn. The simile closely parallels Kautilya (Arthashastra 5.4), who likens royal service to life in fire, and Dhaumya’s counsel in the Mahabharata that the king is a great fire. The traditional sandhi text reads “அகலா தணுகாது” and “விகல்வேந்தர்”, which divide into the same words.

tamil:
மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை மன்னரால்
மன்னிய ஆக்கந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Mannar vizhaipa vizhaiyaamai mannaraal
Manniya aakkam tharum.
current_meaning: If you do not want the things the king himself wants, the king will give you success that lasts.
elementary: Picture a class helper who never tries to grab the teacher’s special chair or the teacher’s favourite pen. Because the teacher never has to worry about that helper, the teacher trusts them more and more. Not wanting what belongs to the boss is how you earn lasting trust.
university: The couplet turns on the repeated root vizhai (to desire): the servant must not desire (vizhaiyaamai) what the kings desire (mannar vizhaipa). Parimelazhagar takes the objects to be the king’s own enjoyments, such as his ornaments, pleasures and women, which a courtier must never share or rival. Mu. Varadarasanar instead reads “those whom the king favours”, meaning one should not compete for the king’s favourites. Either way, the reward is manniya aakkam, prosperity that lasts (manniya = enduring), and it comes through the king himself (mannaraal). The play on mannar/manniya is typical of Valluvar’s sound patterning. The older text in thirukkural-thamizh.org reads மன்னரான் for மன்னரால், a dialectal instrumental ending with the same meaning.

tamil:
போற்றின் அரியவை போற்றல் கடுத்தபின்
தேற்றுதல் யார்க்கும் அரிது.
transliteration:
Potrin ariyavai potral kaduththapin
Thetrudhal yaarkkum aridhu.
current_meaning: If you want to stay safe, avoid serious mistakes. Once the king becomes suspicious of you, no one can make him trust you again.
elementary: A glass vase with a crack can be glued, but you can always see the crack. Trust works the same way. It is much easier to be careful and never break it than to try to fix it after someone starts to doubt you.
university: The first line plays on potru (to guard, to preserve): potrin (if you would guard [yourself]) and potral (guard against). Ariyavai are, in Parimelazhagar’s gloss, grave faults the king will find hard to pardon. The key word is kaduththal, to suspect or to be incensed, and the second line states the psychology bluntly: once suspicion has formed, thetrudhal (reassuring or convincing) is difficult for anyone (yaarkkum). The Kural’s wider theory of trust helps here. Chapter 51 (Therindhu Thelidhal) warns the king against doubting a servant he has tested, so this couplet gives the courtier’s side of the same danger. The sandhi text in older editions runs “போற்றி னரியவை” and “றேற்றுதல் யார்க்கு மரிது.”

tamil:
செவிச்சொல்லும் சேர்ந்த நகையும் அவித்தொழுகல்
ஆன்ற பெரியா ரகத்து.
transliteration:
Sevichchollum serndha nakaiyum aviththozhukal
Aandra periyaar akaththu.
current_meaning: When you are with great and powerful people, do not whisper in someone's ear or share a secret smile with anyone.
elementary: Imagine you are speaking to the class and two children in the front row start whispering and giggling. You would wonder whether they were laughing at you. That is why, around important people, you should not whisper or trade secret smiles.
university: Sevichchol is literally ‘ear-speech’, words whispered into another person’s ear, and serndha nakai is ‘joined laughter’, a smile or glance shared with someone else. Solomon Pappaiah glosses it as winking and smiling while looking at another’s face. The verb avi (to extinguish or suppress) asks the courtier to put out these impulses altogether. Aandra periyaar are ‘the great ones who are complete in power’, which Parimelazhagar takes as kings. The rule rests on the suspicion theme of the previous couplet: private signals between courtiers look to a ruler like conspiracy or mockery. Kautilya’s Arthashastra 5.4 lists almost the same prohibitions, secret talk with another in the assembly and loud laughter without cause. The older text reads “செவிச்சொல்லுஞ் சேர்ந்த நகையு மவித்தொழுக / லான்ற பெரியா ரகத்து.”

tamil:
எப்பொருளும் ஓரார் தொடரார்மற் றப்பொருளை
விட்டக்கால் கேட்க மறை.
transliteration:
Epporulum oraar thodaraarmatru apporulai
Vittakkaal ketka marai.
current_meaning: When the king is talking in secret, do not try to listen in or ask him about it. Hear the secret only if he chooses to tell you.
elementary: When your parents are talking quietly in the kitchen, it is tempting to sneak up and listen, or to keep asking ‘What were you talking about?’ The polite and trustworthy thing is to wait. If they want you to know, they will tell you.
university: The couplet sets out three stages. Oraar means not listening intently or eavesdropping (oru = to attend closely). Thodaraar means not following up with questions. Vittakkaal ketka means listening only once the king himself lets the matter out. The final word, marai (secret, hidden counsel), is held back to the end, which gives the line a sense of withheld information. Parimelazhagar sets the scene as a king in secret counsel with others, and the logic follows from 693: curiosity about royal secrets is exactly what breeds suspicion. The joined text in older editions reads “எப்பொருளு மோரார் தொடரார்மற் றப்பொருளை / விட்டக்காற் கேட்க மறை.”

tamil:
குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி வெறுப்பில
வேண்டுப வேட்பச் சொலல்.
transliteration:
Kurippu arindhu kaalam karudhi veruppila
Venduba vetpach cholal.
current_meaning: Understand the king's mood, wait for the right time, and then say what is needed in a pleasant way he will want to hear.
elementary: If you want to ask for a later bedtime, you would not ask when Mum is rushing or cross. You would wait until she is relaxed, ask kindly, and explain why it is a good idea. Choosing the right moment and the right words makes people ready to listen.
university: The couplet lays out three steps. Kurippu arindhu means reading the ruler’s inner disposition from outward signs, the subject of the very next chapter (71, Kurippu Arithal). Kaalam karudhi means weighing the right time, echoing chapter 49 (Kaalam Arithal). Then comes the manner of speech: veruppila (things not repugnant) and venduba (things needed or useful), spoken vetpa (so that he desires to hear them). Parimelazhagar notes that what is needful must still be said, but framed so that it is welcome. That makes this not flattery but an art of timing and packaging, close to what Greek rhetoric called kairos. The traditional text is the same apart from sandhi.

tamil:
வேட்பன சொல்லி வினையில எஞ்ஞான்றும்
கேட்பினும் சொல்லா விடல்.
transliteration:
Vetpana solli vinaiyila egngnaandrum
Ketpinum sollaa vidal.
current_meaning: Tell the king things that are worth wanting. Never speak of useless things, even if he asks you to.
elementary: If your friend asks you to help them copy homework, a good friend says no, even though the friend asked. A good helper suggests things that really help, and stays quiet about bad ideas, even when invited to share them.
university: Vetpana means ‘what is desirable’, which in Parimelazhagar’s reading are things beneficial to the king, not merely things he would like to hear. Vinaiyila means ‘what has no deed’, that is, fruitless or unprofitable matters. The concessive ketpinum (‘even if he asks’) is the moral centre of the couplet: the courtier’s integrity must hold even against a direct royal request, and egngnaandrum (at no time whatever) rules out exceptions. Commentators differ here. Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as ‘speak only what the king desires’, while Solomon Pappaiah reads ‘speak useful things even unasked’. Pope’s ‘speak pleasant things’ softens the point. The couplet thus protects 696 from being read as a licence to flatter. The older text reads “வினையில வெஞ்ஞான்றுங் / கேட்பினுஞ் சொல்லா விடல்.”

tamil:
இளையர் இனமுறையர் என்றிகழார் நின்ற
ஒளியோடு ஒழுகப் படும்.
transliteration:
Ilaiyar inamuraiyar endru ikazhaar nindra
Oliyodu ozhukap padum.
current_meaning: Do not look down on the king, thinking 'he is younger than me' or 'he is my relative.' Act with respect for the high place he holds.
elementary: Suppose your older cousin becomes the team captain. At family dinners they are just your cousin, but on the field you listen to them as captain. The job deserves respect, whoever is doing it.
university: The couplet names two excuses for disrespect: ilaiyar (‘he is our junior’) and inamuraiyar (‘he stands in such-and-such a kinship relation to us’). Ikazhaar forbids the contempt that comes from both. The key phrase is nindra oli, ‘the radiance that abides [in him]’. Parimelazhagar interprets it as the divine light or majesty present in the king, and Pope accordingly translates ‘the glory kingly state doth bring’. Modern readers such as Solomon Pappaiah reduce it to respect for the office (padhavi) rather than the person. The idea that royal dignity belongs to the office, not the age or family of its holder, closely matches Manusmriti 7.8. The couplet is also a warning to royal kinsmen, whose familiarity is the most tempting route to contempt.

tamil:
கொளப்பட்டேம் என்றெண்ணிக் கொள்ளாத செய்யார்
துளக்கற்ற காட்சி யவர்.
transliteration:
Kolappattem endru ennik kollaadha seyyaar
Thulakkatra kaatchiyavar.
current_meaning: People with steady judgment never think 'the king likes us' and then do things the king would not accept.
elementary: Being the teacher’s favourite does not mean you can break the rules. A sensible student knows that being liked is not a free pass, and keeps behaving well so that the trust lasts.
university: The couplet pivots on two forms of kol (to take, to accept). Kolappattem means ‘we have been accepted or esteemed [by the king]’, and kollaadha means ‘things [he] would not accept’. The echo makes the point that acceptance by the king does not make the unacceptable acceptable. Thulakkatra kaatchi, ‘vision without wavering’, marks the wise courtier as one whose judgement does not drift once favour arrives. Parimelazhagar reads the error as a specific psychology: favour breeds presumption, and presumption breeds offence. That links the couplet forward to 700, where old familiarity replaces present favour as the source of self-deception. The couplet also refines 692: not coveting what is the king’s includes not coveting the licence that favour seems to give.

tamil:
பழையம் எனக்கருதிப் பண்பல்ல செய்யும்
கெழுதகைமை கேடு தரும்.
transliteration:
Pazhaiyam enak karudhip panpalla seyyum
Kezhudhakaimai kedu tharum.
current_meaning: Being too relaxed because 'we are old friends of the king,' and then behaving badly, will lead a person to ruin.
elementary: Suppose your best friend from kindergarten becomes the class president. If you start bossing them around or ignoring the rules because ‘we go way back’, the friendship and your place will both suffer. Old friendship is precious, but it is not permission to misbehave.
university: Pazhaiyam means ‘we are old [associates]’, and panpalla are ‘things that are not proper conduct’. The subject of the sentence is kezhudhakaimai, the intimate familiarity, or the privilege claimed through intimacy, that leads to such conduct, and it is this that tharum (brings) kedu (ruin). The word matters because chapter 81 (Pazhaimai, ‘Old Friendship’) uses kezhudhakaimai approvingly for the easy freedom old friends allow each other. Valluvar deliberately shows that the same freedom, turned toward a king, becomes fatal. The chapter thus ends where it began: the right distance from the fire is not closed by long acquaintance. The older text reads “பழைய மெனக்கருதிப் பண்பல்ல செய்யுங் / கெழுதகைமை கேடு தரும்.”

tamil:
கூறாமை நோக்கக் குறிப்பறிவான் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
மாறாநீர் வையக் கணி.
transliteration:
Kooraamai nokkak kurippu-arivaan enjnjaandrum
Maaraaneer vaiyak kani.
current_meaning: A person who can look at someone and know what they mean without a word being said is always a jewel to this world surrounded by the sea.
elementary: Imagine your friend comes to school looking quiet and droopy. Nobody says anything, but you notice, sit next to them, and share your snack. You understood without being told. Valluvar says a person who can do that is like a jewel the whole world wears.
university: The chapter opens a sequence in the Amaicciyal (section on ministers) that follows directly on ‘Conduct in the Presence of the King’ (ch. 70): having learned how near to stand, the minister must now learn to read the ruler’s unspoken kurippu (intention, inner purpose shown by outward sign). Parimelazhagar reads the subject as the minister and the object as the king: kooraamai (without his saying it) and nokka (by looking, i.e., at the face and eyes) he knows the intent, and such a man is ani (ornament, jewel) to the vaiyam (earth) whose maaraaneer (never-failing water, the ocean) surrounds it; enjnjaandrum means ‘at all times’. The hyperbole of ‘ornament to the world’ rather than ‘to the court’ signals that this faculty is rare and universally prized. The same title, Kurippu Arithal, reappears as chapter 110 in the Kamattuppal, where lovers read each other’s glances; commentators note the deliberate echo between political and amorous sign-reading. The standard text reads nokka; one online sandhi edition prints நோக்ககிக், evidently a misprint for நோக்கக் (some editions give நோக்கிக், with the same sense).

tamil:
ஐயப் படாஅது அகத்தது உணர்வானைத்
தெய்வத்தோ டொப்பக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Aiyap padaaadhu akaththadhu unarvaanaith
Theyvaththodu oppak kolal.
current_meaning: A person who can know without any doubt what is inside someone else's mind should be thought of as equal to a god.
elementary: Some grown-ups seem to know exactly what you are feeling before you say it, and they are always right. It can feel almost magical. Valluvar says a person who can truly do that deserves to be honoured almost like a god.
university: Aiyap padaaadhu uses alapedai (metrical vowel lengthening, படாஅது for படாது) to stretch ‘without doubting’, stressing certainty rather than guesswork. Akaththadhu is ‘that which is within’ (akam = interior, mind), and unarvaan ‘one who perceives’. Parimelazhagar explains the comparison theyvaththodu oppa (as equal to a deity): to know the heart directly is a faculty proper to the divine, so a man who has it without error shares a divine attribute, though he remains human (Mu. Varadarasanar adds ‘even though he is a man’). Kalaignar makes the logic explicit: if such knowledge belongs to God, the man who has it may be likened to God. The couplet should be read with 701 as a rising scale: ornament to the world, then peer of the gods. No significant textual variants; the sandhi text reads படாஅ தகத்த துணர்வானைத்.

tamil:
குறிப்பிற் குறிப்புணர் வாரை உறுப்பினுள்
யாது கொடுத்தும் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Kurippir kurippunar vaarai uruppinul
Yaadhu koduththum kolal.
current_meaning: People who can read what others mean from the signs on their face are worth getting as helpers, whatever you have to give to win them.
elementary: If a football team finds a player who always knows where a teammate will pass before the ball is kicked, the coach will do almost anything to keep that player. Valluvar says a leader should treat people who read signals the same way.
university: The phrase kurippir kurippu unarvaar is the chapter’s technical formula, repeated in 705: ‘those who perceive the kurippu by means of kurippu’. Parimelazhagar takes the first kurippu as the outward signs (of face and eye) and the second as the inner intention they betray; Pope and Drew follow a further gloss in which the reader uses the indications of his own mind as a key to another’s. Uruppu here means the constituent ‘limbs’ of a kingdom (arasu uruppu: army, people, treasury, ministers, allies, forts, as set out in ch. 39), so yaadhu koduththum kolal is ‘secure them by giving whichever of these is asked’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both read it as ‘giving anything among the country’s possessions’. The advice sits in a long Indian tradition of the king paying any price for an able minister. Uruppu will recur in 704 and 705 in the bodily sense (limbs, sense-organs), a deliberate word-play.

tamil:
குறித்தது கூறாமைக் கொள்வாரோ டேனை
உறுப்போ ரனையரால் வேறு.
transliteration:
Kuriththadhu kooraamaik kolvaarodu enai
Uruppor anaiyaraal veru.
current_meaning: People who understand what others mean without being told, and people who cannot, may look the same, but they are very different.
elementary: Two phones can look exactly the same on the outside, but one has a smart app that understands your voice and the other does not. People are like that too: two people can look alike, but one understands what you mean without words and the other does not.
university: Kuriththadhu is ‘what (someone) has in mind’, and kooraamaik kolvaar ‘those who take it in without its being spoken’. Enai = the others (ஏனை), and uruppu or anaiyar (உறுப்பு ஓர் அனையர்) means ‘alike in limbs’, i.e., in bodily form; aal (ஆல்) is concessive (‘though’), and veru ‘they are different’. Parimelazhagar supplies the implied contrast: they are different in understanding (arivu), so the bodily likeness is misleading. The couplet quietly shifts uruppu from 703’s political ‘limbs of the kingdom’ to the body’s limbs. Commentators link it with the Kural’s repeated claim that the unperceptive are human only in form (compare 993 and the chapter on folly), and with the Sanskrit maxim that intelligence shows itself in grasping what is unsaid. The sandhi text reads ‘யுறுப்போ ரனையரால்’; there are no variants of meaning.

tamil:
குறிப்பிற் குறிப்புணரா வாயின் உறுப்பினுள்
என்ன பயத்தவோ கண்.
transliteration:
Kurippir kurippunaraa vaayin uruppinul
Enna payaththavo kan.
current_meaning: If your eyes cannot read what someone means from the signs they give, what use are your eyes among all the parts of your body?
elementary: What good is a flashlight if you never switch it on? Your eyes are for more than seeing colours and shapes. They are meant to notice when someone is sad, worried or happy. If they never notice that, it is as if the flashlight stays off.
university: The couplet repeats 703’s formula kurippir kurippu unar- in the negative (unaraa vaayin, ‘if they do not perceive’) and turns it on the eye itself. Uruppinul (‘among the organs’) now plainly means the body’s members, and enna payaththavo is a rhetorical ‘of what profit are they?’ Parimelazhagar explains that the eyes are the foremost of the sense-organs, and their special excellence is to catch another’s mind through the signs of face and eye; if they cannot do that they are no better than the other limbs. Drew and Pope render ‘if they cannot by their own indications dive those of another’, reflecting the reading that the eye both shows and reads kurippu. The rhetorical question anticipates 710, where the eye becomes the only measuring rod. The sandhi text reads குறிப்புணரா வாயி னுறுப்பினு / ளென்ன பயத்தவோ கண்.

tamil:
அடுத்தது காட்டும் பளிங்குபோல் நெஞ்சம்
கடுத்தது காட்டும் முகம்.
transliteration:
Aduththadhu kaattum palingupol nenjam
Kaduththadhu kaattum mukam.
current_meaning: Just as clear crystal shows the color of whatever is next to it, the face shows whatever is strongest in the heart.
elementary: Put a clear glass marble next to a red flower and the marble looks red. Put it next to a leaf and it looks green. Your face is like that marble. Whatever feeling is strongest inside you shows through it.
university: Palingu (Sanskrit sphatika) is clear rock-crystal, and aduththadhu kaattum means ‘shows what is next to it’: the crystal has no colour of its own but displays the hue of its neighbour. This is the famous Indian sphatika image (the crystal beside a red japa flower) used in Sankhya and Vedanta for how the pure self seems coloured by what it is near; Valluvar turns it into a psychology of expression. Kaduththadhu is glossed by Parimelazhagar as mikkadhu, ‘what is uppermost or abounding’ (from kadu-, to be intense), so the face shows the dominant feeling, not every passing thought. Mu. Varadarasanar reads ‘what abounds in the heart’, and Pope renders ‘what’s throbbing in the mind’. The couplet grounds the chapter’s claim that kurippu can be read: the face is an honest medium. Sandhi text: பளிங்குபோ னெஞ்சங் / கடுத்தது காட்டும் முகம்.

tamil:
முகத்தின் முதுக்குறைந்தது உண்டோ உவப்பினும்
காயினும் தான்முந் துறும்.
transliteration:
Mukaththin mudhukkuraindhadhu undo uvappinum
Kaayinum thaanmun thurum.
current_meaning: Is anything smarter than the face? Whether a person is happy or angry, the face shows it first.
elementary: When you get a present you love, your smile arrives before you can say ‘thank you’. When you are cross, your frown shows up before any words. Your face is like a messenger who always runs ahead of you.
university: Mudhukkuraindhadhu comes from mudhukkurai(mai), a Tamil idiom for mature wisdom or sagacity (literally ‘old-shortened’, an idiom whose sense is ‘wise beyond years’); the question ‘is there anything wiser than the face?’ credits the face with a kind of intelligence. Uvappinum kaayinum (‘whether it rejoices or burns with anger’) names the two poles of emotion, and thaan mun urum means ‘it comes forward first’, before speech or deliberate action. Parimelazhagar comments that the face runs ahead of the mind in disclosing liking and dislike, which is why it is called wise: it seems to know first. The irony is deliberate: the face is ‘wise’ precisely because it cannot keep a secret. Sandhi text: முதுக்குறைந்த துண்டோ வுவப்பினுங் / காயினுந் தான்முந் துறும்.

tamil:
முகம்நோக்கி நிற்க அமையும் அகம்நோக்கி
உற்ற துணர்வார்ப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Mukamnokki nirka amaiyum akamnokki
Utradhu unarvaarp perin.
current_meaning: If you have people who can look into your heart and understand what has happened to you, it is enough to stand where they can see your face.
elementary: When you come home after a bad day, a good parent can often tell just by looking at you. You don’t have to explain; you just stand there, and they already know you need a hug. Valluvar says that is what great helpers are like.
university: The couplet balances two ‘lookings’: mukam nokki (looking at the face) and akam nokki (looking into the heart). Nirka amaiyum means ‘it suffices to stand’, and utradhu is ‘what has befallen’ (a trouble or need). Parimelazhagar makes the king the one who stands: if he has ministers able to look into his mind and perceive what has occurred, he need not voice his trouble; standing and looking at their faces is enough, and they will understand and remedy it. Some modern readers (e.g., Kalaignar) generalise it to anyone who can read hearts. The couplet is the practical payoff of 701 and 703: the value of the perceptive minister is that the ruler is spared the need to speak, which in court may itself be dangerous. Variant spelling: ytamizh prints முகம்நோக்கி, the sandhi edition முகநோக்கி நிற்க வமையு மகநோக்கி.

tamil:
பகைமையும் கேண்மையும் கண்ணுரைக்கும் கண்ணின்
வகைமை உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Pakaimaiyum kenmaiyum kannuraikkum kannin
Vakaimai unarvaarp perin.
current_meaning: To people who understand the different ways eyes look, the eyes alone will show if someone is an enemy or a friend.
elementary: A dog can tell if you are friendly by the way you look at it. Soft eyes mean ‘friend’, a hard stare means ‘watch out’. Wise people learn to read eyes the same way, and the eyes tell them who is a friend and who is not.
university: Pakaimai (enmity) and kenmai (friendship, intimacy) are the two things kan uraikkum, ‘the eye will declare’. The condition is kannin vakaimai unarvaar, ‘those who perceive the varieties (vakai) of the eye’, i.e., the different kinds of look. Parimelazhagar applies it to foreign policy: if the king has ministers who can read the movements of the eye, the eyes of other kings and their envoys will themselves reveal hostility or friendship. Drew’s translation, following him, adds ‘(of foreign kings)’. Commentators link the verse with the Kural’s treatment of hidden enmity (ch. 89, Utpakai) and false friendship (ch. 83), where a smiling face may cover hostility: the eye is harder to disguise than the mouth. Sandhi text: பகைமையுங் கேண்மையுங் கண்ணுரைக்குங் கண்ணின் / வகைமை யுணர்வார்ப் பெறின்.

tamil:
நுண்ணியம் என்பார் அளக்குங்கோல் காணுங்கால்
கண்ணல்லது இல்லை பிற.
transliteration:
Nunniyam enpaar alakkungol kaanungaal
Kannalladhu illai pira.
current_meaning: If you look closely at people who say they can read others well, you will find their only measuring stick is the eyes. They use nothing else.
elementary: A builder uses a ruler to measure wood. A person who is good at understanding others uses a different ruler: their eyes. By watching carefully, they measure what someone is feeling.
university: Nunniyam enpaar are ‘those who say, we are subtle (nunmai)’, i.e., who claim fine discernment. Alakkungol is ‘the rod with which they measure’ (alakkum kol), and kaanungaal ‘when one examines it’. Parimelazhagar, as usual, applies it to ministers: the measuring rod of those who claim to know others’ minds turns out, on inspection, to be nothing but their eyes. There is a double sense that commentators note: the minister measures by his own eye, and what he measures is the other person’s eye (continuing 709). The closing kan alladhu illai pira (‘there is nothing other than the eye’) sums up the chapter, which moves from praise of the perceptive (701-704) to the face (706-707) and finally the eye (705, 709-710) as the decisive sign. Sandhi text: நுண்ணிய மென்பா ரளக்குங்கோல் காணுங்காற் / கண்ணல்ல தில்லை பிற.

tamil:
அவையறிந்து ஆராய்ந்து சொல்லுக சொல்லின்
தொகையறிந்த தூய்மை யவர்.
transliteration:
Avaiyarindhu aaraaindhu solluka sollin
Thokaiyarindha thooimai yavar.
current_meaning: People with clean minds who know the power of words should first understand the group they are speaking to, and then speak with care.
elementary: You talk one way to your baby cousin, another way to your friends, and another way to your teacher. A good speaker first looks at who is listening, then picks the right words for them.
university: The chapter opens by making knowledge of the audience (avai, the assembly or council) a precondition of speech: avaiyarindhu (having known the assembly) comes before aaraaindhu (having deliberated) and solluka (let them speak). Parimelazhagar explains that assemblies are of three grades relative to the speaker, those superior, equal, and inferior in learning (mikkaar, oththaar, thaazhndhaar), and the rest of the chapter works through how to behave before each. Sollin thokai (the aggregate of words) is glossed in the commentarial tradition, and in Solomon Pappaiah’s modern paraphrase, as the three kinds of expressive word: direct (senjol), figurative (ilakkanai-chol), and suggestive (kurippu-chol). Thooimai (purity) is a moral term, not a stylistic one: the speaker must not use this command of language to deceive the hearers. The ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net texts print the first word as “அவையறிநது”, an evident typing slip; the sandhi-joined text “அவையறிந் தாராய்ந்து” confirms the reading அவையறிந்து ஆராய்ந்து.

tamil:
இடைதெரிந்து நன்குணர்ந்து சொல்லுக சொல்லின்
நடைதெரிந்த நன்மை யவர்.
transliteration:
Idaitherindhu nankunarndhu solluka sollin
Nadaitherindha nanmai yavar.
current_meaning: Good people who know how words work should choose the right moment, understand the subject fully, and only then speak.
elementary: If you want to ask your mom for something, you don’t ask while she is rushing to catch a bus. You wait for a good moment and think it through first. Wise speakers wait for the right time too.
university: Where 711 stressed the audience, this kural stresses the moment: idai (interval, opening) is glossed by Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar as the court’s sevvi, its receptive moment, when the hearers are ready and willing to listen. Nankunarndhu (having understood well) requires full command of the matter, and Solomon Pappaiah adds that the speaker must avoid faults of both word and sense (sorkutram, porutkutram). Sollin nadai (the gait or course of words) refers to how each of the three kinds of word conveys its meaning, which parallels sollin thokai in 711. The parallel structure of 711 and 712 (sollin thokaiyarindha thooimaiyavar / sollin nadaitherindha nanmaiyavar) presents purity and goodness as twin moral qualities of the ideal counsellor. The text is the same in all sources consulted, apart from the sandhi joining (“சொல்லி னடைதெரிந்த”).

tamil:
அவையறியார் சொல்லல்மேற் கொள்பவர் சொல்லின்
வகையறியார் வல்லதூஉம் இல்.
transliteration:
Avaiyariyaar sollalmer kolpavar sollin
Vakaiyariyaar valladhooum il.
current_meaning: People who start speaking without understanding their listeners do not know how words work. They have no real skill at all.
elementary: Imagine telling a scary ghost story at a little kid’s birthday party. The story may be good, but you picked the wrong crowd, and now everyone is crying. Not knowing your listeners can spoil even good words.
university: This kural is the negative of 711. Avaiyariyaar (those who do not know the assembly) who take up speaking (sollal mer kolpavar) are thereby shown to be sollin vakaiyariyaar, ignorant of the kinds of words. Valladhooum il (they have no ability whatever) uses an alapedai, a lengthened vowel (thooum), for emphasis. Parimelazhagar’s point is that eloquence cannot be separated from knowledge of the audience. A speaker who misjudges the assembly proves thereby that he does not know how words work, however learned he may be. The sandhi text reads “சொல்லன்மேற் கொள்பவர்”, and “வல்லதூஉ மில்”, which divide into the same words as சொல்லல்மேற் and வல்லதூஉம் இல்.

tamil:
ஒளியார்முன் ஒள்ளிய ராதல் வெளியார்முன்
வான்சுதை வண்ணம் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Oliyaarmun olliya raadhal veliyaarmun
Vaansudhai vannam kolal.
current_meaning: Among bright, learned people, show how bright you are. Among dull people, be plain like a white-painted wall and do not show off.
elementary: With your older brother who loves science, you can talk about planets and black holes. With your little sister you just say “the moon is pretty tonight.” You are just as smart either way. You simply show only as much as your listener can use.
university: The kural depends on a pun: oliyaar (the luminous, the learned) is set against veliyaar (the blank or white, the empty-minded), and before the latter one should take on the colour of vaansudhai, pure white lime plaster. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read this as appearing unlearned before the unlearned. Solomon Pappaiah softens it to coming down to the hearers’ level so that they can follow, and Kalaignar keeps the stronger sense of appearing ignorant. Plaster is bright but has no lustre of its own, so the image suggests someone who covers his learning without losing his integrity. This is the key verse of the chapter’s three-way scheme (superior, equal, inferior assemblies), and it is the source of the modern Tamil proverbial advice to “be white lime before fools.” The text agrees in all sources; the sandhi text reads “ஒளியார்முன் னொள்ளிய ராதல்” and “வண்ணங் கொளல்”.

tamil:
நன்றென்ற வற்றுள்ளும் நன்றே முதுவருள்
முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு.
transliteration:
Nandrendra vatrullum nandre mudhuvarul
Mundhu kilavaach cherivu.
current_meaning: Of all good things, the best is holding back from speaking first when you are among elders who are wiser than you.
elementary: When your grandparents and their friends are talking about the old days, you might know a fun fact too. But the polite and smart thing is to listen first and let them speak. Waiting your turn shows you are growing up.
university: Mudhuvar are elders in knowledge, not just in age. In Parimelazhagar’s scheme this is the conduct suited to an assembly superior to oneself, just as 714’s first half suits an equal one. Mundhu kilavaa means not uttering (kila, to speak) first, not jumping ahead. Cherivu (literally density or closeness) here means self-restraint, what Mu. Varadarasanar calls adakkam, and it links this chapter to ch. 13, Adakkamudaimai. The superlative nandrendravatrullum nandre (good even among the things called good) is strong praise: such restraint is ranked above other virtues of the counsellor. Kalaignar’s paraphrase adds a vivid Tamil idiom, “like a cashew seed” (mundhiri kottai), for a person who pushes forward to speak. The text agrees across sources; the sandhi text reads “நன்றென்ற வற்றுள்ளு நன்றே முதுவருண்”.

tamil:
ஆற்றின் நிலைதளர்ந் தற்றே வியன்புலம்
ஏற்றுணர்வார் முன்னர் இழுக்கு.
transliteration:
Aatrin nilaithalarndh thatre viyanpulam
Etrunarvaar munnar izhukku.
current_meaning: Making a mistake in speech in front of people who understand many subjects is like slipping and falling off the right path.
elementary: A spelling mistake in a note to your friend is no big deal. The same mistake in the final round of a spelling bee, in front of the judges, feels like tripping on stage. Mistakes count most in front of experts.
university: Viyanpulam (wide fields, meaning vast areas of learning) etrunarvaar (those who have received and understood them) are the most demanding audience there is, and an izhukku (slip or lapse) before them is compared to aatrin nilaithalarndhatru, losing one’s footing on the way. Commentators disagree about aaru. Parimelazhagar and most modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) take it as the path of right conduct, so a verbal slip before the learned is as disgraceful as a good man’s moral lapse. Puliyur Kesikan takes aaru as a river and reads the image as a swimmer losing his footing mid-stream, so the lapse is dangerous and hard to recover from. The kural thus explains why 715’s restraint matters: before the learned the cost of error is very high. The text agrees in all sources; the sandhi text reads “ஆற்றி னிலைதளர்ந் தற்றே வியன்புல மேற்றுணர்வார் முன்ன ரிழுக்கு”.

tamil:
கற்றறிந்தார் கல்வி விளங்கும் கசடறச்
சொல்தெரிதல் வல்லார் அகத்து.
transliteration:
Katrarindhaar kalvi vilangum kasadarach
Soltheridhal vallaar akaththu.
current_meaning: The learning of people who have studied deeply shines brightest among those who can judge words without any mistakes.
elementary: A great chess move looks like nothing special to someone who doesn’t know chess. Show it to a chess champion and they gasp, “Wow!” Your best work shines most in front of people who can understand it.
university: Vilangum (will shine, become manifest) is the key verb. Learning does not show its worth in a vacuum. It becomes visible only in the akam (midst, company) of those who are kasadara soltheridhal vallaar, able to examine words kasadara, without flaw or dross. Kasadu (impurity, dross) links back to Valluvar’s famous command in ch. 40, Kalvi (kural 391): “கற்க கசடறக் கற்பவை.” There is a pairing here: flawless study (391) meets flawless hearing (717). Commentators note that this kural balances 716. The expert audience that punishes a slip is also the only audience that can properly recognise real learning. The ytamizh/thirukkural.net text “சொல்தெரிதல்” and the sandhi form “சொற்றெரிதல்” are the same word.

tamil:
உணர்வ துடையார்முன் சொல்லல் வளர்வதன்
பாத்தியுள் நீர்சொரிந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Unarva thudaiyaarmun sollal valarvadhan
Paaththiyul neersorindh thatru.
current_meaning: Speaking to people who can understand is like watering a garden bed where plants are already growing.
elementary: Watering a plant that is already sprouting makes it shoot up fast. Watering an empty patch of dirt does nothing. Telling good ideas to someone who wants to learn is like watering the sprout.
university: This kural is the positive counterpart of the chapter’s closing image (720). Unarvadhu udaiyaar are people who have understanding, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah stress that they understand for themselves (thaame unargindra), even without being told. Speaking to them is like watering (neer sorindhatru) a paaththi, a small irrigated garden bed, in which the crop is valarvadhu, already growing of its own accord. The image is agricultural and exact: the water does not create growth but speeds up growth that is already under way, so the speaker’s words bear fruit at once. Parimelazhagar takes this as the assembly of equals in learning, and so completes the scheme begun in 714. The text agrees across sources; the sandhi text reads “உணர்வ துடையார்முற் சொல்லல்” and “பாத்தியு ணீர்சொரிந் தற்று”.

tamil:
புல்லவையுள் பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லற்க நல்லவையுள்
நன்கு செலச்சொல்லு வார்.
transliteration:
Pullavaiyul pochchaandhum sollarka nallavaiyul
Nanku selach chollu vaar.
current_meaning: People who can speak good things well to a good group should never, even by mistake, speak about them to a low-minded group.
elementary: You wouldn’t show your best drawing to kids who you know will just scribble on it and laugh. Save it for people who will really look at it. Good words should be shared with good listeners.
university: Pullavai (a low or mean assembly, from pul, grass, meaning petty or base) is set against nallavai (a good assembly). Pochchaandhum (even through forgetfulness) uses the root of ch. 54, Pochchaavaamai (Unforgetfulness): the speaker is not to slip, even for a moment, into speaking before an unworthy audience. Nanku sela sollu (to speak so that it goes in well) describes speech that enters and settles in the hearers’ minds. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as speech that is “fixed in the mind” (manadhil padhiyumaaru). The ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net texts print “நன்குசலச்”, apparently a corruption. The sandhi text “நன்கு செலச்சொல்லு வார்” and P. A. Muthukrishnan’s musical setting (“நன்கு செலச் சொல்லுவார்”, quoted on thirukkural.net) support the reading செல, which Parimelazhagar’s gloss (to cause to enter) also requires.

tamil:
அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்தற்றால் தங்கணத்தார்
அல்லார்முன் கோட்டி கொளல்.
transliteration:
Anganaththul ukka amizhdhatraal thanganaththaar
Allaarmun kotti kolal.
current_meaning: Speaking to people who are not like-minded is like spilling amrita (the drink that makes gods live forever) into a dirty drain.
elementary: Imagine pouring the most delicious juice in the world down the drain. What a waste! Explaining something wonderful to people who don’t care at all is like that. The juice was good; it just went to the wrong place.
university: The chapter closes with its most memorable image. Amizhdhu (amrita, the nectar of immortality) is ukka (spilled) into an anganam, the drain of a house’s open courtyard: Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss it as an unclean courtyard, Solomon Pappaiah as a sewer. Thanganaththaar allaar are those who are not of one’s own gana (group, circle), meaning not one’s equals in learning and outlook. Kotti kolal (to hold a discourse) uses kotti, cognate with Sanskrit goshthi (assembly, learned conversation). The simile, like 718’s, is exact. Nectar is not spoiled by being spilled, but it can never be recovered or drunk, so it is wasted. The sources differ slightly on one form: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read தங்கணத்தார், while the sandhi-joined text reads “தங்கணத்த ரல்லார்முற்” (தங்கணத்தர்). The meaning is unaffected.

tamil:
வகையறிந்து வல்லவை வாய்சோரார் சொல்லின்
தொகையறிந்த தூய்மை யவர்.
transliteration:
Vakaiyarindhu vallavai vaaisoraar sollin
Thokaiyarindha thooimai yavar.
current_meaning: People with pure minds who know the power of words and understand their listeners will not stumble when they speak before a powerful group.
elementary: Imagine you know every line of the school play, and you have peeked out to see who is in the audience. Because you know your words and you know who is listening, your voice stays steady. Knowing your words and knowing your listeners keeps you from getting tongue-tied.
university: This couplet opens Avaiyañcāmai (“not fearing the assembly”). It pairs with the chapter before it, Avaiyaṟital (knowing the assembly), inside the Amaicciyal, the section on ministers. Parimelazhagar reads vakai aṟintu (“knowing the kind”) as first working out what sort of assembly one is in. Vallavai is the assembly of the able or powerful, and vāy sōrār means “their mouths will not slip,” that is, they will not falter or make mistakes out of fear. Sollin tokai aṟinda tūymaiyavar are “the pure who know the tokai (range or classification) of words,” which commentators connect with a grammarian’s knowledge of word-classes and how to use them. So the chapter’s first answer to stage fright is skill combined with integrity. The sandhi-joined text reads “சொல்லின் றொகையறிந்த,” where றொ is simply ன் fused with தொ, and the words are unchanged.

tamil:
கற்றாருள் கற்றார் எனப்படுவர் கற்றார்முன்
கற்ற செலச்சொல்லு வார்.
transliteration:
Katraarul katraar enappaduvar katraarmun
Katra selachchollu vaar.
current_meaning: People who can share what they have learned with other learned people, in a way that really reaches them, are called the most learned of all.
elementary: Lots of kids can read a book. The one who can explain it clearly to the whole class, even with the teacher listening, is the one everyone calls the real expert.
university: The line repeats kaṟṟār (“the learned”) four times. The word-play mirrors the idea that learning is measured among the learned. The key term is cela-c-colluvār, “those who speak so that it goes (cel-)” into the hearers. Parimelazhagar glosses it as speaking so that the matter enters the listeners’ minds, and Mu. Varadarasanar likewise says “so that it settles in their hearts.” The judgement is about rank: standing among scholars comes from being able to explain things well before one’s peers, not from private learning. The sandhi-joined text reads “கற்றாருட் கற்றா ரெனப்படுவர் கற்றார்முற்,” in which ட் and ற் are sound-changes of ள் and ன் before க.

tamil:
பகையகத்துச் சாவார் எளியர் அரியர்
அவையகத்து அஞ்சா தவர்.
transliteration:
Pakaiyakaththuch chaavaar eliyar ariyar
Avaiyakaththu anjaa thavar.
current_meaning: Many people are ready to die fighting among enemies. Few people can stand in front of a group and speak without fear.
elementary: Lots of people are brave in a game or on the playground. Standing up in front of the whole school to say what you really think takes a different kind of courage, and fewer people have it.
university: The couplet is built as a sharp contrast: pakai-y-akattu (“inside the enemy ranks”) against avai-y-akattu (“inside the assembly”), and eḷiyar (“easy to find, many”) against ariyar (“rare”). Parimelazhagar takes the first group as warriors who throw themselves fearlessly among the enemy and die, and the second as those who are unafraid before the learned. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the first as “many in the world.” The couplet ranks civil courage above martial courage, a bold claim in a culture whose puṟam poetry celebrated heroic death. The sandhi-joined text “பகையகத்துச் சாவா ரெளிய ரரிய / ரவையகத் தஞ்சா தவர்” divides into the same words.

tamil:
கற்றார்முன் கற்ற செலச்சொல்லித் தாம்கற்ற
மிக்காருள் மிக்க கொளல்.
transliteration:
Katraarmun katra selachchollith thaamkatra
Mikkaarul mikka kolal.
current_meaning: Share what you have learned with learned people so it reaches them. Then learn from those who know more the things you do not yet know.
elementary: Share what you know in class. Then listen to the teacher and the older kids who know even more. Speaking up and listening both help you grow.
university: The couplet repeats the formula kaṟṟār mun kaṟṟa cela-c-colli from 722 and adds a second duty: mikkāruḷ mikka koḷal, “take the surplus from those who surpass you.” Parimelazhagar reads mikkār as those superior in learning and mikka as whatever their learning holds beyond one’s own. The ytamizh commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) agree. Speaking before the learned is therefore not a performance but one part of a cycle of learning: speak, be tested, learn more. The sandhi-joined text has “தாங்கற்ற” and “மிக்காருண்” for தாம்கற்ற and மிக்காருள்.

tamil:
ஆற்றின் அளவறிந்து கற்க அவையஞ்சா
மாற்றங் கொடுத்தற் பொருட்டு.
transliteration:
Aatrin alavarindhu karka avaiyanjaa
Maatrang koduththar poruttu.
current_meaning: Study the right way to reason and argue, so that you can answer questions in front of a group without fear.
