elementary: If you want to answer tricky questions without getting nervous, practise thinking things through step by step. When you know how to reason, a hard question doesn’t scare you.
university: Parimelazhagar reads āṟṟin aḷavu aṟintu kaṟka as “learn, by the proper path (of grammar), the aḷavai-nūl,” that is, the science of pramāṇa (means of valid knowledge), or logic. Solomon Pappaiah paraphrases it as tarka śāstra, the logic of proofs, and Kalaignar as grammar together with logic. Māṟṟam koṭuttal means “giving a reply,” so the purpose of this study is avai añcā, not fearing the assembly, above all when being cross-questioned. Some modern readers take āṟṟin aḷavu more loosely as “the measure of one’s ability” or “the scope of the subject.” The sandhi text “ஆற்றின் னளவறிந்து” shows a metrical doubling, and the words are the same.

tamil:
வாளொடென் வன்கண்ணர் அல்லார்க்கு நூலொடென்
நுண்ணவை அஞ்சு பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Vaalodden vankannar allaarkku noolodden
Nunnavai anju pavarkku.
current_meaning: What use is a sword to someone who is not brave? What use are books to someone afraid of a group of sharp thinkers?
elementary: A shiny sword is no use to a knight who runs away. In the same way, knowing lots of facts doesn’t help if you’re too scared ever to say them.
university: Two parallel questions, vāḷoṭu eṉ (“what [has he] to do with a sword?”) and nūloṭu eṉ (“what with books?”), set weapons and learning side by side. Vaṉkaṇ, literally “hard eye,” means steady courage. Nuṇ-avai is an assembly of subtle, sharp minds. Solomon Pappaiah takes nūl specifically as books of logic, continuing from 725, while Kalaignar reads it broadly as learning in general. On all readings the logic is the same: just as a sword is useful only to the brave, learning is useful only to someone who can use it before the learned. Owning it without using it is the same as not owning it. The sandhi text reads “வன்கண்ண ரல்லார்க்கு நூலொடெ / னுண்ணவை யஞ்சு பவர்க்கு.”

tamil:
பகையகத்துப் பேடிகை ஒள்வாள் அவையகத்து
அஞ்சு மவன்கற்ற நூல்.
transliteration:
Pakaiyakaththup pedikai olvaal avaiyakaththu
Anju mavankatra nool.
current_meaning: The learning of someone who is afraid to speak in front of a group is like a shiny sword in the hand of a coward facing the enemy.
elementary: Picture a very sharp, shiny sword held by someone who is shaking too hard to lift it. It looks impressive but does nothing. Learning you’re too scared to share is just like that sword.
university: This couplet turns 726 into a single simile: pēṭi kai oḷ vāḷ, “the bright sword in the hand of a pēṭi.” In classical Tamil, pēṭi means a person who is neither man nor woman, traditionally glossed as a eunuch or hermaphrodite. Pope and Drew translate it “hermaphrodite,” and Pope’s verse has “sexless being.” The martial culture of the time used such a person as a stock figure for someone unfit for battle; the image reflects that period’s assumptions, not a judgement the modern reader needs to share. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all stress uselessness: the sword is fine, but the hand fails it. The couplet also repeats 723’s pakai-y-akattu / avai-y-akattu frame. The sandhi text reads “பேடிகை யொள்வா ளவையகத் / தஞ்சு மவன்கற்ற நூல்.”

tamil:
பல்லவை கற்றும் பயமிலரே நல்லவையுள்
நன்கு செலச்சொல்லா தார்.
transliteration:
Pallavai katrum payamilare nallavaiyul
Nanku selachchollaa thaar.
current_meaning: No matter how many subjects they have studied, people who cannot share good things clearly with a good group are of no use.
elementary: A treasure chest that stays locked forever is no better than an empty box. If you learn lots of things but never share them clearly, nobody gets any good out of them.
university: The couplet plays on the syllable avai: pal-l-avai (“many things”) and nal-l-avai (“a good assembly”) echo each other. Payam ilar means “without benefit.” Here payam is the classical form of payaṉ (use, fruit), not the modern Tamil word for fear, a false friend worth pointing out in a chapter about fear. Nalla avai is the assembly of good or learned people, and naṉku cela-c-collutal again means speech that reaches and persuades (see 722). Solomon Pappaiah adds that such a person is useless to the world, extending the loss from the individual to society. The sandhi text reads “நல்லவையு / ணன்கு.”

tamil:
கல்லா தவரின் கடையென்ப கற்றறிந்தும்
நல்லா ரவையஞ்சு வார்.
transliteration:
Kallaa thavarin kadaiyenba katrarindhum
Nallaa ravaiyanju vaar.
current_meaning: People who have studied and understood, yet are afraid to speak before a group of good people, are said to be even lower than people who never learned.
elementary: If a kid knows the answer but stays quiet because they’re scared, it’s as if they never knew it. It might even be worse, because a kid who doesn’t know can at least ask a question.
university: Kaṭai means “the lowest,” so kallātavariṉ kaṭai is “lower than the unlearned.” The verb eṉpa (“they say”) presents the judgement as the verdict of the wise. Kaṟṟu aṟintum, “though they have learned and understood,” stresses both study and understanding, so the failure is purely a failure of nerve. Solomon Pappaiah reads avai añcuvār as those so afraid that they do not even go to the assembly. The ranking is harsh because the unlearned at least lack the means, while the learned coward wastes what he has. Variant: thirukkural-thamizh’s sandhi text reads “கல்லா தவரிற் கடையென்ப கற்றறிந்து / நல்லா ரவையஞ்சு வார்,” where the final -um of கற்றறிந்தும் is absorbed before ந; ytamizh prints the separated form கற்றறிந்தும்.

tamil:
உளரெனினும் இல்லாரொடு ஒப்பர் களன்அஞ்சிக்
கற்ற செலச்சொல்லா தார்.
transliteration:
Ulareninum illaarodu oppar kalananjik
Katra selachchollaa thaar.
current_meaning: People who fear a group and so cannot share what they have learned in a way that reaches others are like the dead, even though they are alive.
elementary: A lamp that is never switched on might as well not be there. When fear stops you from ever sharing what you know, it is as if that part of you isn’t there at all.
university: Uḷar eṉiṉum (“though they exist, are alive”) and illārotu oppar (“they are equal to those who are not”) set being against non-being. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read illār as the dead. Kaḷaṉ (kaḷam, “arena, place of assembly”) stands in for avai for variety, and añci (“fearing”) names the cause. The closing phrase kaṟṟa cela-c-collātār repeats the formula of 722 and 724 and ties the chapter together: to learn but not to pass it on is a kind of death. The sandhi text reads “உளரெனினு மில்லாரொ டொப்பர் களனஞ்சிக்.”

tamil:
தள்ளா விளையுளும் தக்காரும் தாழ்விலாச்
செல்வரும் சேர்வது நாடு.
transliteration:
Thallaa vilaiyulum thakkaarum thaazhvilaach
chelvarum servadhu naadu.
current_meaning: A true country has three things together: crops that never fail, good and worthy people, and rich people whose riches do not shrink.
elementary: Think of a good neighbourhood. The gardens always grow food, there are wise grown-ups you can ask for help, and the shopkeepers do well enough to keep their shops open. When all three are there together, it feels like a real home. Valluvar says a country is the same.
university: The chapter opens the Kural’s treatment of naadu (the realm or territory), the third of the six angas (limbs) of kingship listed in kural 381, and it begins with a definition by constituents. Thallaa vilaiyul is literally ‘produce that does not fail’ (thal, to reject or fall off), thakkaar are ‘the worthy’, whom Parimelazhagar glosses as men of virtue and learning, and thaazhvilaa chelvar are ‘the wealthy without decline’, whom he identifies as merchants whose stock never runs out; Pope’s prose gloss follows him in naming merchants. Modern commentators widen the reading: Solomon Pappaiah turns the first term into the labourers who produce the harvest and the third into the unselfish rich, while Kalaignar reads the wealthy as those who do not squander riches on evil ends. The verb servadhu (that in which they gather together) makes the point that a land is defined by the coexistence of these groups, not by any one of them. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘விளையுளுந் தக்காருந்’ and ‘செல்வருஞ்’, which divide into the same words.

tamil:
பெரும்பொருளால் பெட்டக்க தாகி அருங்கேட்டால்
ஆற்ற விளைவது நாடு.
transliteration:
Perumporulaal pettakka thaaki arungettaal
aatra vilaivadhu naadu.
current_meaning: A true country is so rich that others want it, is free from terrible disasters, and grows plenty of crops.
elementary: Imagine a garden so lovely and full of fruit that everyone in town wishes it were theirs. It is not flooded or eaten by pests, and every year it gives more than enough. That is what a good country is like.
university: Perumporul is ‘great wealth’, and pettakkadhu means ‘that which is desirable’; Parimelazhagar takes the desire to be that of other kingdoms, so the kural admits that a rich land will be coveted, which prepares for the next chapter on fortification (Aran). Arungettaal is read by Parimelazhagar as arum-kedu, ‘with destructive causes being absent’ (arumai here meaning scarcity or absence), and Solomon Pappaiah lists the traditional calamities meant: excessive rain, drought, wild beasts, harmful birds and misrule. Aatra vilaivadhu means ‘yielding abundantly’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read pettakkadhu more generally as ‘praised and desired by all’. The sandhi-joined text runs the words together as ‘பெட்டக்க தாகி யருங்கேட்டா லாற்ற’, with no change in meaning.

tamil:
பொறையொருங்கு மேல்வருங்கால் தாங்கி இறைவற்கு
இறையொருங்கு நேர்வது நாடு.
transliteration:
Poraiyorungu melvarungaal thaangi iraivarku
iraiyorungu nervadhu naadu.
current_meaning: A true country can carry heavy burdens that fall on it all at once, and still pay its ruler all the taxes it owes.
elementary: Picture a strong family. When cousins suddenly arrive because their house was flooded, the family makes room and shares its food, and it still pays its bills on time. A good country is strong in the same way.
university: Porai is ‘burden’ and orungu ‘all together’, so the first line describes a load that arrives all at once. Parimelazhagar specifies the load as people fleeing from neighbouring lands in distress, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow him, Pappaiah adding refugees from war and natural disaster. The second line plays on the double sense of irai: iraivan is the king and irai is the tax due to him, so a land ‘yields fully the king’s due to the king’ (iraivarku irai orungu nervadhu). The kural therefore measures a country’s strength by its surplus, since only a land with reserves can absorb strangers and still pay its revenue gladly. The sandhi text reads ‘மேல்வருங்காற் றாங்கி யிறைவற் கிறையொருங்கு’, the same words joined.

tamil:
உறுபசியும் ஓவாப் பிணியும் செறுபகையும்
சேரா தியல்வது நாடு.
transliteration:
Urupasiyum ovaap piniyum serupakaiyum
seraa thiyalvadhu naadu.
current_meaning: A true country carries on free from terrible hunger, diseases that never end, and enemies that destroy.
elementary: A happy home is one where nobody goes to bed hungry, nobody is sick all the time, and nobody is afraid of bullies breaking in. Valluvar says a good country is a whole land like that.
university: The kural names the classic triad of public calamity: urupasi (severe hunger, famine), ovaap pini (disease that does not cease, that is, epidemic) and serupakai (enemies who destroy). Parimelazhagar notes that the third means enemies who come from outside and attack, since internal enmity is treated separately in the next kural. The verb iyalvadhu (that which goes on, continues) suggests a lasting condition rather than a single lucky year. The same trio of famine, pestilence and war recurs in Sanskrit, biblical and Greek accounts of disaster, which makes this one of the most widely shared ideas in the chapter. The sandhi text reads ‘உறுபசியு மோவாப் பிணியுஞ் செறுபகையுஞ்’.

tamil:
பல்குழுவும் பாழ்செய்யும் உட்பகையும் வேந்தலைக்கும்
கொல்குறும்பும் இல்லது நாடு.
transliteration:
Palkuzhuvum paazhseyyum utpakaiyum vendhalaikkum
kolkurumpum illadhu naadu.
current_meaning: A true country has no groups fighting each other, no enemies inside who bring ruin, and no killer gangs that trouble the king.
elementary: A sports team can have the best players, but if they split into little groups that fight each other, and some even help the other side, they will lose. A country is the same: it needs its people to pull together.
university: Where kural 734 dealt with dangers from outside, this one turns to dangers from within. Palkuzhu is ‘many groups’, which Parimelazhagar reads as factions that quarrel among themselves, paazhseyyum utpakai is ‘internal enmity that works ruin’, and vendhalaikkum kolkurumpu is ‘murderous petty chiefs (or bands) that harass the king’; kurumpu can mean a small hill-chief or a gang of marauders. Solomon Pappaiah modernises the list as caste, religious and political factions, disloyal party members, and local strongmen. The theme is developed fully in chapter 89 (Utpakai, Internal Enmity). The ytamizh text prints the last word as ‘இல்லத’, which appears to be a typographical slip for the standard ‘இல்லது’ found in the sandhi text and other editions.

tamil:
கேடறியாக் கெட்ட இடத்தும் வளங்குன்றா
நாடென்ப நாட்டின் தலை.
transliteration:
Kedariyaak ketta idaththum valangundraa
naadenpa naattin thalai.
current_meaning: Wise people say the best country is one that never meets ruin, and even when harm does come, does not lose its riches.
elementary: A strong tree is rarely hurt by storms, and even when a branch breaks, it keeps giving fruit. The best country is like that tree: hardly ever harmed, and quick to stay fruitful even when it is.
university: The kural has two degrees of excellence: kedariyaa (‘not knowing ruin’) and, failing that, ketta idaththum valam kundraa (‘even when ruined, its richness does not decline’). Parimelazhagar takes the ruin to be damage from enemies, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow him, while Kalaignar reads it as any kind of harm that the land’s resources are great enough to repair. Enpa (‘they say’) marks the judgment as the view of the learned, and naattin thalai means ‘the head, or foremost, of lands’. The idea is resilience: the best land is judged not only by its good years but by how it comes through bad ones. The ytamizh text reads ‘நாட்டின் தலை’ and the sandhi text ‘நாட்டிற் தலை’, a difference of joining only.

tamil:
இருபுனலும் வாய்ந்த மலையும் வருபுனலும்
வல்லரணும் நாட்டிற்கு உறுப்பு.
transliteration:
Irupunalum vaaindha malaiyum varupunalum
vallaranum naattirku uruppu.
current_meaning: The parts of a country are water from rain and from springs, hills in the right places, rivers that flow from them, and a strong fort.
elementary: A castle in a story often sits by a river, with hills behind it, springs nearby and high walls around it. Water keeps people alive, and hills and walls keep them safe. Valluvar says a country needs all of these, like a body needs arms and legs.
university: Uruppu means ‘limb’ or ‘organ’, so the kural presents the natural features of a land as parts of a living body. Parimelazhagar reads irupunal (‘the two waters’) as water from below (springs, wells) and water from above (rain), and varupunal (‘the water that comes’) as rivers flowing from the hills; the hills themselves are vaaindha (well situated) because they feed the rivers and shelter the land. Kalaignar instead reads irupunal as river and sea, and varupunal as rain. Vallaran, the ‘strong fortress’, anticipates the next chapter, Aran, where hills, water and forest reappear as natural defences. The sandhi text reads ‘வல்லரணு நாட்டிற் குறுப்பு’.

tamil:
பிணியின்மை செல்வம் விளைவின்பம் ஏமம்
அணியென்ப நாட்டிற்கிவ் வைந்து.
transliteration:
Piniyinmai selvam vilaivinpam emam
aniyenpa naattirkiv vaindhu.
current_meaning: Wise people say a country has five jewels: no disease, riches, good crops, happiness and safety.
elementary: A birthday cake looks best with candles, icing, fruit, sprinkles and a name on top. A country has its own five decorations: healthy people, enough money, good crops, happy faces and safe streets.
university: Ani means ‘ornament’ or ‘jewel’, so where kural 737 listed the land’s limbs (uruppu), this one lists its adornments. The five are piniyinmai (absence of disease), selvam (wealth), vilaivu (produce), inpam (enjoyment, happiness) and emam (safety, protection); Parimelazhagar glosses emam as the protection given to subjects. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pope follow the same five, while some modern readers join vilaivu and inpam as ‘the joy of harvest’. The verse sums up the chapter’s positive ideal in a single list. The ytamizh text prints the second line as ‘அணியென்ப நாட்டிவ் வைந்து’, but the sandhi text and the standard editions read ‘நாட்டிற்கிவ் வைந்து’ (naattirku + iv + aindhu, ‘these five for a land’), which is needed for the metre and is followed here.

tamil:
நாடென்ப நாடா வளத்தன நாடல்ல
நாட வளந்தரு நாடு.
transliteration:
Naadenpa naadaa valaththana naadalla
naada valandharu naadu.
current_meaning: Wise people say a true country is one whose riches come without having to search for them. A land that gives riches only after hard searching is not a true country.
elementary: Some gardens grow fruit almost by themselves because the soil and rain are just right. Other gardens need you to dig, water and fight weeds every day for a tiny crop. Valluvar says the best country is like the first garden.
university: The kural is built on a pun between naadu (‘country’) and the verb naadu (‘to seek, to search for’): naadaa valaththana are lands ‘whose wealth is not sought’, and naada valandharu naadu is a land ‘that gives wealth only when sought’. Parimelazhagar explains that the best lands produce their riches by natural endowment, without great exertion by the inhabitants, while lands that yield only to heavy labour are not counted as countries in the full sense. The line is not a praise of idleness, since the Kural elsewhere (chapter 62, Aalvinaiyudaimai) insists on effort; it is a judgment on natural endowment. Kalaignar makes this explicit by contrasting lands naturally rich with lands that prosper only through constant struggle.

tamil:
ஆங்கமை வெய்தியக் கண்ணும் பயமின்றே
வேந்தமை வில்லாத நாடு.
transliteration:
Aangamai veydhiyak kannum payamindre
vendhamai villaadha naadu.
current_meaning: Even if a land has all these good things, it is of no use if it does not have a good king who gets along with his people.
elementary: You can have the best football, the greenest field and the fastest players, but without a good captain who works well with the team, you will not win. A country with every treasure still needs a good leader.
university: The chapter ends by subordinating everything it has praised to kingship. Aangu amaivu eydhiya kannum means ‘even when it has attained all the excellences set out there’ (in the previous nine kurals), and payam indre means ‘it is without fruit’. The key compound vendhamaivu is read by Parimelazhagar as ‘harmony, or fitness, between king and subjects’, which Pope follows with ‘not with its king at peace’; Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar and Sivayogi Sivakumar read it more simply as ‘a good king or good government’, and Solomon Pappaiah as a government with love for its citizens. Either way, the verse links this chapter back to the Kural’s section on kingship (Arasiyal) and warns that natural wealth without right rule is wasted. The sandhi text agrees with ytamizh word for word.

tamil:
ஆற்று பவர்க்கும் அரண்பொருள் அஞ்சித்தற்
போற்று பவர்க்கும் பொருள்.
transliteration:
Aatru pavarkkum aranporul anjiththar
potru pavarkkum porul.
current_meaning: A fort is a treasure both for a king who goes out to attack and for a king who stays inside it to protect himself out of fear.
elementary: Think of a tree house with a strong ladder. When you want to go out and play a game of tag, it is your safe base to run out from. When it starts to rain or a big dog chases you, it is the place you run back into. Valluvar says a fort is useful in both ways, for going out and for staying safe.
university: The chapter opens the Kural’s treatment of aran (fortification), the last of the six angas (limbs) of the state listed in kural 381 (padai, kudi, koozh, amaichu, natpu, aran). The couplet is built on a balanced contrast: aatrupavar are ‘those who act’, which Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) take as those who go out to make war on others, while anjith than potrupavar are ‘those who, fearing, guard themselves’, the besieged who seek shelter. The word porul is used twice, first as ‘a thing of value’ (aran porul, ‘the fort is a treasure’) and then as the predicate, a deliberate play on the same word that also names the whole second book of the Kural (Porutpaal). The point is that a fortress is not merely defensive: it is a base of operations for offense and a refuge in weakness alike. The sandhi-joined text on thirukkural-thamizh.org reads ‘ஆற்று பவர்க்கு மரண்பொரு ளஞ்சித்தற்’, which divides into the same words as the ytamizh.com text.

tamil:
மணிநீரும் மண்ணும் மலையும் அணிநிழற்
காடும் உடைய தரண்.
transliteration:
Maninheerum mannum malaiyum aninizhar
kaadum udaiya tharan.
current_meaning: A true fort has water as clear as a jewel, open land, hills, and a forest with thick shade.
elementary: Imagine building a pillow fort. It is best to put it behind the sofa, beside a blanket ‘river’, with a big armchair ‘mountain’ next to it and lots of cushions like a forest. Anyone sneaking up has to cross all of that first. Valluvar says the best forts use nature in the same way: water, open ground, hills and forest.
university: Here Valluvar lists the natural defenses (iyarkai aran) that should surround a fort: mani neer (water clear as a gem, i.e. a moat or lake that never dries), mann (land, glossed by Varadarasanar and Pappaiah as open ground with no cover for an attacker), malai (hill) and ani nizhal kaadu (forest of beautiful or dense shade). Parimelazhagar and the later commentators read these as four types of fort: neer aran, nila aran, malai aran and kaattu aran. Pappaiah states this directly. The list closely parallels the Sanskrit arthashastra classification into water-fort (audaka), mountain-fort (parvata), desert or open-land fort (dhanvana) and forest-fort (vanadurga), which suggests a shared South Asian military science that the next couplet calls simply ‘the treatise’ (nool). Kalaignar reads mani neer as a deep, wide moat. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘மணிநீரு மண்ணு மலையு மணிநிழற் / காடு முடைய தரண்’, which divides into the same words.

tamil:
உயர்வகலம் திண்மை அருமைஇந் நான்கின்
அமைவரண் என்றுரைக்கும் நூல்.
transliteration:
Uyarvakalam thinmai arumaiin naankin
amaivaran endruraikkum nool.
current_meaning: Books on this subject say a fort's wall must have four things: height, thickness, strength, and be hard to get to.
elementary: A good sandcastle wall has to be tall so the waves can’t jump over it, thick so they can’t push through, packed hard so it doesn’t crumble, and hard to reach, maybe behind a ditch. If any one of these is missing, the sea gets in. Valluvar says the old books on forts ask for the same four things.
university: After the natural defenses (742), Valluvar turns to the man-made wall (seyarkai aran, as Pappaiah calls it) and gives its four standard qualities: uyarvu (height, so that it cannot be scaled), akalam (breadth, which Pappaiah explains as room for defenders to stand and move on the rampart), thinmai (solidity, so that it cannot be battered down) and arumai (difficulty or inaccessibility). Parimelazhagar’s tradition explains arumai as the difficulty of approach created by engines and traps (pori) set on the walls, a reading that Pappaiah follows. The phrase endru uraikkum nool, ‘so says the treatise’, is one of the places where Valluvar openly cites earlier military and political science. Commentators link it to the arthashastra tradition, whose fort specifications (for example, a rampart ‘six dandas high and twice as much broad’) are very similar. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘உயர்வகலந் திண்மை யருமையிந் நான்கி / னமைவர ணென்றுரைக்கு நூல்’.

tamil:
சிறுகாப்பிற் பேரிடத்த தாகி உறுபகை
ஊக்கம் அழிப்ப தரண்.
transliteration:
Sirukaappir peridaththa thaaki urupakai
ookkam azhippa tharan.
current_meaning: A fort should have only a few places that need guarding but lots of room inside, and it should crush the spirit of any enemy that attacks.
elementary: Think of a playground fort with just one small doorway and lots of room inside. You only need one friend at the door to keep watch, while everyone else can play inside. And anyone who tries to get in soon gives up, because the doorway is so hard to rush. That is Valluvar’s kind of fort.
university: The couplet sets two design principles against each other: siru kaappu (small guard-length, i.e. few places that need to be defended) and per idam (large interior space). The commentators all explain this as a narrow, easily held perimeter or entrance around a spacious interior; Kalaignar says that the part to be protected is small while the inside is wide. The second line gives the purpose: urupakai ookkam azhippathu, ‘that which destroys the zeal of the strong enemy who comes against it’. Pappaiah glosses this as filling the besiegers with dismay. The idea is psychological as much as structural: a well-designed fort defeats the attacker’s morale before it defeats his army. Parimelazhagar treats the chapter’s verses from 743 on as a list of the defining marks (ilakkanam) of a man-made fort. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘சிறுகாப்பிற் பேரிடத்த தாகி யுறுபகை / யூக்க மழிப்ப தரண்’.

tamil:
கொளற்கரிதாய்க் கொண்டகூழ்த் தாகி அகத்தார்
நிலைக்கெளிதாம் நீரது அரண்.
transliteration:
Kolarkarithaaik kondakoozhth thaaki akaththaar
nilaikkelithaam neerathu aran.
current_meaning: A fort should be hard to capture, full of stored food, and easy for the people inside to defend.
elementary: If you are playing a long game of capture-the-flag, your base needs three things. It should be hard for the other team to get into, it should have snacks and water so you don’t have to leave, and it should be easy for your own team to move around in. Valluvar says a real fort needs the same three things.
university: The couplet names three conditions. Kolarku arithaai means ‘hard to take’; Pappaiah adds ‘even under a siege of many days’. Konda koozhthu aagi means ‘holding provisions’. Koozh (literally gruel or food) is the same word that names the Koozhiyal (the section on wealth and resources) in some divisions of the Porutpaal, and here it means stored food. Akaththaar nilaikku elithaam means ‘easy for those within to hold their position’. Varadarasanar reads this as easy for the defenders to stay in, while Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as convenient for the defenders to fight from. The final neerathu (‘of such a nature’) marks the three conditions as the fort’s defining nature. The ytamizh text reads ‘நிலைக்கெளிதாம் நீரது’, and the sandhi-joined text on thirukkural-thamizh.org reads ‘நிலைக்கெளிதா நீர தரண்’. These are orthographic variants of the same words.

tamil:
எல்லாப் பொருளும் உடைத்தாய் இடத்துதவும்
நல்லாள் உடையது அரண்.
transliteration:
Ellaap porulum udaiththaai idaththuthavum
nallaal udaiyathu aran.
current_meaning: A true fort has everything that may be needed, and good, brave soldiers who will help when danger comes.
elementary: A good school on a stormy day has torches, blankets and food in the cupboard. But it also needs calm grown-ups who know what to do when the lights go out. Supplies alone are not enough; you need good people too. Valluvar says the same about a fort.
university: The first line (ellaap porulum udaiththaai, ‘having all things’) sums up the material requirements of 745, and the second line brings in the human element that the chapter’s last couplet will make decisive: idaththu uthavum nallaal, ‘good men who help at the (critical) place or time’. Idam can mean both the spot where danger arises and the moment of need, and Varadarasanar reads it as the moment of crisis in battle. Nallaal (nal + aal, ‘good person’) is read by all the commentators as brave warriors: Pappaiah speaks of heroes who can defeat enemies trying to destroy the fort from outside, and Kalaignar of strong fighters who leap into battle. The pairing of stores and soldiers reflects the arthashastra and Dharmashastra habit of listing a fort’s supplies and its garrison together. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘எல்லாப் பொருளு முடைத்தா யிடத்துதவு / நல்லா ளுடைய தரண்’.

tamil:
முற்றியும் முற்றா தெறிந்தும் அறைப்படுத்தும்
பற்றற் கரியது அரண்.
transliteration:
Mutriyum mutraa therindhum araippaduththum
patrar kariyathu aran.
current_meaning: A true fort cannot be taken by surrounding it, by attacking it directly, or by tricks from people inside.
elementary: Imagine your best toy locked in a treasure box. Someone might wait outside your room for hours, or try to grab it quickly, or even trick your little brother into opening the box. A really safe box beats all three tricks. Valluvar says a real fort must be safe from waiting, grabbing and tricking.
university: The couplet lists the three ways a fort can be taken and says a true aran resists all of them: mutriyum (by besieging it all round), mutraathu erindhum (by attacking without a full siege, i.e. storming a weak point), and araippaduththum (by araippadal, which Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read as vanjanai, deceit or treachery, and Pappaiah as turning some of those inside into a fifth column). Pope’s English (‘mine beneath the ground’) follows the other old sense of arai as a hollow or underground passage, so there is a real divergence between treachery and undermining; the Tamil commentarial tradition generally prefers treachery. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘முற்றியு முற்றா தெறிந்து மறைப்படுத்தும்’, where ‘எறிந்து மறைப்படுத்தும்’ is the sandhi form of ‘எறிந்தும் அறைப்படுத்தும்’, which confirms the reading araippaduththum. The inclusion of treachery points ahead to 750: the human element can undo even a physically perfect fort.

tamil:
முற்றாற்றி முற்றி யவரையும் பற்றாற்றிப்
பற்றியார் வெல்வது அரண்.
transliteration:
Mutraatri mutri yavaraiyum patraatrip
patriyaar velvathu aran.
current_meaning: A true fort lets the people inside, holding their ground, beat even a strong army that is skilled at surrounding forts.
elementary: In a game of king-of-the-hill, the one on top can hold off a crowd of climbers as long as he keeps his footing. Valluvar says a good fort works like that hill. Even when many skilled attackers surround it, the defenders who hold their ground can win.
university: The couplet repeats two roots in a tight pattern. Mutraatri mutriyavar means ‘those who besiege, being skilled (aatri) in besieging’, i.e. an expert siege force, and patraatrip patriyaar means ‘those who hold on, being able to hold (their ground)’, i.e. the defenders who do not let go of the place they occupy. Varadarasanar reads patru as the defenders’ attachment to their position, and Pappaiah as not abandoning their post. The fort is defined by its result: it is that in which the holders defeat (velvathu) even a skilled besieger. The repeated sounds (mutru, patru) make the couplet memorable. It shifts the chapter from the fort’s structure to the fort in action, preparing for 749-750. The sandhi-joined text on thirukkural-thamizh.org is ‘முற்றாற்றி முற்றி யவரையும் பற்றாற்றிப் / பற்றியார் வெல்வ தரண்’, which matches ytamizh.com.

tamil:
முனைமுகத்து மாற்றலர் சாய வினைமுகத்து
வீறெய்தி மாண்ட தரண்.
transliteration:
Munaimukaththu maatralar saaya vinaimukaththu
veereythi maanda tharan.
current_meaning: A true fort becomes famous because its fighters are so skilled that they knock down the enemy right at the front line.
elementary: A castle becomes famous not just because its walls are pretty but because of the brave defenders who stopped every attack at the gate. People tell stories about what they did there. Valluvar says a fort gets its greatness from the deeds done in its defense.
university: The couplet sets munaimukam (the battle-front) against vinaimukam (the field of action or operations): the enemy (maatralar) falls (saaya) at the front because of what the defenders do, and through those deeds the fort attains distinction (veeru eythi) and excellence (maanda). Pappaiah notes that the enemy is destroyed ‘as soon as battle begins’, and Kalaignar stresses attacks launched from within. Veeru, ‘pride, distinction, uniqueness’, suggests that a fort’s fame comes from the deeds done in its defense rather than from its stones. The couplet is thus the bridge between the structural couplets (742-747) and the conclusion in 750 that without vinai maatchi (excellence in action) no fort exists at all. The repetition of mukaththu (‘at the face of’) in both halves is a characteristic Kural device. The sandhi-joined text is identical in wording to the ytamizh.com reading.

tamil:
எனைமாட்சித் தாகியக் கண்ணும் வினைமாட்சி
இல்லார்கண் இல்லது அரண்.
transliteration:
Enaimaatchith thaakiyak kannum vinaimaatchi
illaarkan illathu aran.
current_meaning: No matter how great a fort is, it is no fort at all if the people in it are not skilled and strong in action.
elementary: You could have the best football in the world, but if nobody on your team can kick, you will still lose. A fort is the same. The tallest walls are useless if the people inside don’t know how to defend them. Valluvar ends the chapter by saying that people matter more than walls.
university: The closing couplet undercuts everything before it. Enai maatchiththu aakiya kannum means ‘even when it has every kind of excellence’, summing up the natural defenses, walls, provisions and garrison of 742-749. Yet it is illathu, ‘non-existent’, among those who lack vinai maatchi, excellence in action. Varadarasanar glosses vinai maatchi as skill in the ways of action, Pappaiah as the ability to understand and act against the enemy, and Kalaignar simply says that if those inside are incompetent there is no use at all. The play on maatchi (‘excellence’) in both lines sets the fort’s excellence against its holders’ excellence, and the holders win. Pope’s verse rendering (‘To craven souls no fortress strength supplies’) makes the lack a matter of courage, while the Tamil commentators stress practical competence more broadly. The ytamizh.com Varadarasanar gloss ends with the words ‘பொருள் செயல்வகை’, the title of the next chapter, which appears to be a page artifact rather than part of the commentary. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘எனைமாட்சித் தாகியக் கண்ணும் வினைமாட்சி / யில்லார்க ணில்ல தரண்’.

tamil:
பொருளல் லவரைப் பொருளாகச் செய்யும்
பொருளல்லது இல்லை பொருள்.
transliteration:
Porulal lavaraip porulaakach cheyyum
porulalladhu illai porul.
current_meaning: Nothing but money can make people who count for nothing into people who count for something. There is nothing else like it.
elementary: Imagine a boy nobody picks for the team. One day he brings a brand-new football, and suddenly everyone wants to play with him. He is the same boy, but now people notice him. Valluvar says money works like that ball: it makes people who were ignored get noticed.
university: The chapter opens the Kural’s treatment of koozh (கூழ், treasury or wealth), one of the six limbs of the state named in kural 381, and it begins with a deliberately startling claim. The couplet plays on three senses of porul: ‘thing of account’, ‘worth’, and ‘wealth’, so that porulallavar are ‘those who are no-thing’, and the second line says there is no porul (thing) except porul (wealth). Parimelazhagar treats the verse as a plain statement of how the world behaves rather than a moral endorsement, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar likewise read it as a description of social esteem, not of true merit. The ytamizh text divides பொருளல்லது இல்லை, while the sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh reads பொருளல்ல தில்லை; the words are the same.

tamil:
இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர் செல்வரை
எல்லாரும் செய்வர் சிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Illaarai ellaarum elluvar selvarai
ellaarum seyvar sirappu.
current_meaning: Everyone looks down on people who have nothing, and everyone praises people who are rich.
elementary: Two children come to a party. One wears a torn shirt and the other a shiny new outfit. Some people smile at the second child and ignore the first, even though nothing else is different. Valluvar is telling us this happens, so that we notice it and do not treat people unfairly.
university: The couplet is built on a tight parallelism: illaarai (the have-nots) against selvarai (the wealthy), and ellaarum elluvar (all scorn) against ellaarum seyvar sirappu (all do honour). Mu. Varadarasanar adds in parentheses that the poor are scorned even if they have other virtues and the rich honoured even if they have none, which makes the verse a comment on injustice as well as a fact of life. Parimelazhagar reads it, like 751, as a reason for the ruler to gather wealth: a king without a treasury would suffer the same contempt. Kalaignar’s gloss calls this simply the way of the world (உலக நடப்பு). The sandhi-joined text reads இல்லாரை யெல்லாரு மெள்ளுவர், which divides into the same words.

tamil:
பொருளென்னும் பொய்யா விளக்கம் இருளறுக்கும்
எண்ணிய தேயத்துச் சென்று.
transliteration:
Porulennum poyyaa vilakkam irularukkum
enniya theyaththuch chendru.
current_meaning: Money is a lamp that never goes out. Take it to any land you choose, and it drives away the darkness there, most of all the darkness of enemies.
elementary: Think of a torch that never runs out of batteries. Wherever you walk at night, it lights the path. Valluvar says money can be like that: when you go to a new place, it can help you make friends and solve problems.
university: The metaphor pairs poyyaa vilakkam (the lamp that does not fail or lie) with iruL (darkness), and the second line sends the lamp to enniya theyam, ‘the country one has in mind’ (theyam from Sanskrit desha). Parimelazhagar glosses the darkness as enmity (பகையாகிய இருள்), and Pope and Drew’s English follows him with ‘the darkness (of enmity)’; Solomon Pappaiah likewise says wealth enters even foreign lands and dispels the darkness of hostility. Mu. Varadarasanar reads iruL more broadly as any obstacle (இடையூறு), and Kalaignar as suffering (துன்பம்). The verse sets up 759, where wealth becomes the sharpest weapon against a foe’s pride. The sandhi-joined text reads விளக்க மிருளறுக்கு மெண்ணிய, which divides into the same words.

tamil:
அறன்ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும் திறனறிந்து
தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்.
transliteration:
Aran eenum inbamum eenum thiranarindhu
theedhindri vandha porul.
current_meaning: Money earned the right way, without doing anything wrong, brings both goodness and happiness.
elementary: Imagine two children selling lemonade. One makes it carefully and charges a fair price. The other sneaks sugar from a neighbour and cheats customers. Only the first can enjoy the money without worry and use it to do kind things. Valluvar says honest money brings both goodness and happiness.
university: The verb eenum (ஈனும், ‘brings forth, gives birth to’) is repeated for both aram (virtue) and inbam (pleasure or happiness), so wealth is pictured as the parent of the other two purusharthas. The conditions are thiran arindhu, ‘knowing the proper means’, and theedhu indri, ‘without evil’. Parimelazhagar takes the proper means to be those fitting one’s station and the law, and the absence of evil to mean acquiring without harm or deceit to others. Sivayogi Sivakumar adds that it means seeking wealth with knowledge of one’s own ability and harming no one. The sandhi-joined text reads அறனீனு மின்பமு மீனுந், which divides into the same words.

tamil:
அருளொடும் அன்பொடும் வாராப் பொருளாக்கம்
புல்லார் புரள விடல்.
transliteration:
Arulodum anbodum vaaraap porulaakkam
pullaar purala vidal.
current_meaning: Do not hold on to money that comes without kindness and love. Let it go.
elementary: Suppose you could win a big prize, but only by being mean to a friend. Valluvar says to let that prize go. Money that makes you unkind is like a shiny apple that is rotten inside.
university: The first line names two qualities the earning must carry: arul (அருள், compassion toward all beings, the subject of chapter 25) and anbu (அன்பு, affection toward one’s own, the subject of chapter 8). The second line is vivid: pullaar, ‘not embracing’ (from pullu, to hug or cling), and purala vidal, ‘letting it roll off’, as one lets go of something that slips from the arms. Parimelazhagar applies the verse to the ruler, who should refuse revenue gathered by cruelty to his subjects, and Pope and Drew’s English accordingly begins with ‘(Kings) should rather avoid’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah generalise it to anyone who earns. The sandhi-joined text reads அருளொடு மன்பொடும், which divides into the same words.

tamil:
உறுபொருளும் உல்கு பொருளும்தன் ஒன்னார்த்
தெறுபொருளும் வேந்தன் பொருள்.
transliteration:
Uruporulum ulgu porulumthan onnaarth
theruporulum vendhan porul.
current_meaning: A king’s money comes from property that has no owner, from taxes on goods and roads, and from payments made by enemies he has beaten.
elementary: Think of a school fund. It gets money from lost-and-found items nobody claims, from small fees for using the playground, and from the prize when the school wins a match against another school. Valluvar lists the kinds of money that belong to a king’s treasury in a similar way.
university: This is the chapter’s one technical verse, listing three lawful sources of royal revenue. Uruporul is ‘wealth that comes of itself’, which Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah explain as ownerless property such as heirless estates and treasure trove, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take it as ordinary tax (இறை, வரி). Ulgu porul is customs or toll revenue on goods, and theru porul is tribute or spoil taken from subdued enemies (onnaar). The verse spells out what 755 means in practice: a king’s legitimate income has clear, lawful channels. The sandhi-joined text reads உறுபொருளு முல்கு பொருளுந்தன் னொன்னார்த், which divides into the same words.

tamil:
அருளென்னும் அன்பீன் குழவி பொருளென்னும்
செல்வச் செவிலியால் உண்டு.
transliteration:
Arulennum anbeen kuzhavi porulennum
selvach cheviliyaal undu.
current_meaning: Kindness is the child born to love, and it is brought up by a rich nanny called money.
elementary: Picture a baby born to a loving mother, cared for by a kind nanny who has plenty of food and warm blankets. Valluvar says kindness is like that baby: love gives birth to it, and money helps it grow, because it is easier to help others when you have something to give.
university: This is one of the Kural’s finest extended metaphors. Arul (compassion for all beings) is the kuzhavi, the infant, born of anbu (love for one’s own; anbeen is anbu plus eenra, ‘borne by love’), and porul is the selvach cheviliyal, the rich wet-nurse or foster-mother (cevili) who raises it. The genealogy reverses the usual worry that wealth corrupts: love begets compassion, but compassion cannot grow into practical kindness without means. It links back to chapter 8, Anbudaimai, which says love begets affection and friendship, and it answers 755 by showing the right relation of wealth to arul and anbu. The sandhi-joined text reads அருளென்னு மன்பீன் குழவி பொருளென்னுஞ், which divides into the same words.

tamil:
குன்றேறி யானைப்போர் கண்டற்றால் தன்கைத்தொன்று
உண்டாகச் செய்வான் வினை.
transliteration:
Kundreri yaanaippor kandatraal thankaiththondru
undaagach cheyvaan vinai.
current_meaning: Starting a job with money already in hand is like watching an elephant fight from a hilltop. You are safe and can see everything.
elementary: Imagine two huge elephants pushing and fighting in a field. If you stood in the middle, you could get hurt. But if you climb a hill and watch from the top, you are safe and can see everything. Valluvar says that starting a big job with savings in your pocket is like watching from that hill.
university: The simile draws on a familiar sight in Sangam India, the royal elephant fight, which was deadly to anyone on the ground and a pleasure to watch from high up. Thankaiththu ondru undaaga means ‘with something being in one’s own hand’, that is, having one’s own funds, and cheyvaan vinai is ‘the work of one who acts’. Parimelazhagar explains that such a person has no need to depend on others and so can watch the struggle of the undertaking without fear, while Kalaignar adds the image of not being caught between the fighting elephants. The sandhi-joined text reads கண்டற்றாற் றன்கைத்தொன் றுண்டாகச், which divides into the same words.

tamil:
செய்க பொருளைச் செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும்
எஃகதனிற் கூரிய தில்.
transliteration:
Seyga porulaich cherunar serukkarukkum
eqkadhanir kooriya thil.
current_meaning: Build up your money. No blade is sharper than money for cutting down the pride of your enemies.
elementary: Imagine a bully who brags that nobody can stand up to him. Then the whole class saves up to build a strong new fence and hire a coach, and suddenly the bully stops bragging. Valluvar says a well-stocked treasury is the sharpest sword against a proud enemy.
university: The verse opens with a blunt imperative, seyga porulai, ‘make wealth!’, which is rare in the Kural and gives the command its force. Cherunar are foes, serukku is their arrogance, and aRukkum (‘that cuts off’) sets up the image of eqku (எஃகு), steel or a sword, of which nothing is sharper (kooriyadhu il). Parimelazhagar explains that wealth lets a king raise and keep armies and allies, and so humbles enemies without his having to strike himself. Solomon Pappaiah addresses the verse to anyone who wants to achieve something. The sandhi-joined text reads செருக்கறுக்கு மெஃகதனிற், which divides into the same words.

tamil:
ஒண்பொருள் காழ்ப்ப இயற்றியார்க்கு எண்பொருள்
ஏனை இரண்டும் ஒருங்கு.
transliteration:
Onporul kaazhppa iyatriyaarkku enporul
enai irandum orungu.
current_meaning: For people who have earned plenty of money honestly, the other two goals of life, doing good and being happy, come easily.
elementary: Think of a garden. Once the soil is rich and well watered, flowers and vegetables both grow easily. Valluvar says honest wealth is like that rich soil: once you have it, goodness and happiness grow easily too.
university: The closing verse ties the chapter to the three aims of life (muppaal: aram, porul, inbam) that give the Kural its three books. Onporul is ‘bright’ or excellent wealth, which the commentators take to mean wealth gained by good means, echoing 754; kaazhppa (from kaazh, hard core) means firmly and abundantly; enporul is ‘an easy thing’ (en, easy); and enai irandum orungu means ‘the other two, together’. Parimelazhagar explains that for such a person virtue and pleasure are both easily attained, and Kalaignar names the three purusharthas explicitly. The verse repeats the pairing in 754 and closes the chapter’s argument that honestly earned wealth underpins a complete life. The sandhi-joined text reads இயற்றியார்க் கெண்பொரு ளேனை யிரண்டு மொருங்கு, which divides into the same words.

tamil:
உறுப்பமைந்து ஊறஞ்சா வெல்படை வேந்தன்
வெறுக்கையுள் எல்லாம் தலை.
transliteration:
Uruppamaindhu ooranjaa velpadai vendhan
verukkaiyul ellaam thalai.
current_meaning: An army that has every part it needs and wins without fear of getting hurt is the greatest treasure a king can own.
elementary: Think of a school sports team where every position is filled, everyone has practised, and nobody is scared of a hard game. A coach would say that team is worth more than any trophy cupboard. Valluvar says a king’s well-prepared army is like that: his most precious possession.
university: The chapter opens the Padai-iyal (the section on the army), and its first couplet ranks the army above every other form of veṟukkai (வெறுக்கை, ‘wealth, treasure’). Uṟuppu (உறுப்பு, ‘limb’) is read by Parimelazhagar as the traditional four limbs of an Indian army, elephants, chariots, horse and foot, so uṟuppamaintu means ‘complete in its divisions’; ūṟu (ஊறு) is ‘wound’ or ‘harm’, and ūṟañcā ‘not dreading injury’. The logic echoes kural 381, which lists the army (படை) first among the six limbs of a kingdom, and the Arthashastra’s list of seven elements of sovereignty. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss the line almost identically; Solomon Pappaiah modernizes the ‘limbs’ as land, sea and air forces and police. The ytamizh and thirukkural-thamizh texts agree, differing only in sandhi (உறுப்பமைந் தூறஞ்சா).

tamil:
உலைவிடத்து ஊறஞ்சா வன்கண் தொலைவிடத்துத்
தொல்படைக் கல்லால் அரிது.
transliteration:
Ulaividaththu ooranjaa vankan tholaividaththuth
tholpadaik kallaal aridhu.
current_meaning: Only an army with a long history has the courage to stand firm after losses, unafraid of wounds even when its numbers have shrunk.
elementary: When a team is losing badly, new players often give up, but players who have trained together for years keep going. They have been through hard games before. Valluvar says an old, experienced army is like that: it keeps its courage even when things are going wrong.
university: Ulaivu (உலைவு) means ‘reverse, setback’ and tolaivu (தொலைவு) ‘diminution, loss of numbers’, so the couplet describes valour (vaṉkaṇ, வன்கண்) that survives both defeat and attrition. Tolpaṭai (தொல்படை, ‘ancient army’) is read by Parimelazhagar as the hereditary core force (often called மூலப்படை in the commentarial tradition), as against hired or allied troops, a distinction that closely parallels Kautilya’s preference for hereditary troops. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar follow this reading, while Solomon Pappaiah extends tolpaṭai to native citizen-soldiers whose families have long lived in the land. The text is identical in both sources apart from sandhi (வன்கண் டொலைவிடத்துத் in the joined text).

tamil:
ஒலித்தக்கால் என்னாம் உவரி எலிப்பகை
நாகம் உயிர்ப்பக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Oliththakkaal ennaam uvari elippakai
naagam uyirppak kedum.
current_meaning: So what if a crowd of rats roars like the sea? One hiss from a cobra and they all run away and are destroyed.
elementary: Imagine a crowd of mice squeaking very loudly in a barn. It sounds scary, but the moment a snake hisses, they all scurry away. Valluvar says a big, noisy army with no real courage is like those mice, and a small, brave army is like the snake.
university: The couplet is a celebrated uvamai (simile): uvari (உவரி, ‘the salt sea’) describes the roar of a vast but timid enemy, while nākam (நாகம், ‘cobra’) and uyirppa (உயிர்ப்ப, ‘as it breathes, hisses’) picture a small force of real valour. Parimelazhagar reads it as a statement that numbers without courage count for nothing against a brave army, and Solomon Pappaiah explicitly makes the cobra a small army and the rats a large one ‘rat-like in mind’. Kalaignar applies it to a single hero rising in anger. The text is the same in both sources apart from sandhi (ஒலித்தக்கா லென்னா முவரி யெலிப்பகை).

tamil:
அழிவின்றி அறைபோகா தாகி வழிவந்த
வன்க ணதுவே படை.
transliteration:
Azhivindri araipogaa thaagi vazhivandha
vankanadhuve padai.
current_meaning: A true army is one that has never been beaten, cannot be bribed by the enemy, and has courage passed down from its fathers.
elementary: Imagine a family that has played in the same village band for generations. Nobody could pay them to play for a rival band, and they never give up halfway through a parade. Valluvar says a true army is like that: loyal, steady, and brave because bravery runs in its history.
university: Three marks define the true army here: aḻiviṉmai (not being broken in battle), aṟaipōkāmai (அறைபோகாமை, not being undermined or won over by enemy intrigue, i.e. free of treachery and desertion), and vaḻivanta vaṉkaṇ (வழிவந்த வன்கண், valour inherited through lineage). Parimelazhagar takes aṟaipōtal as being corrupted by the enemy’s secret approaches, and Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as ‘not falling prey to the enemy’s deceit’. There is a small textual variant: ytamizh prints அழிவின்றி, while the sandhi-joined thirukkural-thamizh text reads அழிவின் றறைபோகா, i.e. அழிவின்று; the sense, ‘without destruction’, is unchanged.

tamil:
கூற்றுடன்று மேல்வரினும் கூடி எதிர்நிற்கும்
ஆற்ற லதுவே படை.
transliteration:
Kootrudandru melvarinum koodi edhirnirkum
aatraladhuve padai.
current_meaning: A true army is one that can stand together and fight even if Death himself comes at it in anger.
elementary: Picture a group of friends holding hands in a line during a strong wind on the beach. Alone, each might be pushed over, but together they stay standing. Valluvar says a real army stands together like that, even against the scariest danger.
university: Kūṟṟu (கூற்று) is Death personified, identified by commentators with Yama, and uṭaṉṟu (உடன்று) means ‘having become enraged’. The key word is kūṭi (கூடி, ‘together, united’): the excellence praised is collective resolve rather than individual heroism, and āṟṟal (ஆற்றல்) is the strength to hold. Parimelazhagar notes that even the god of death cannot be resisted by ordinary means, so the hyperbole stresses unity as the army’s defining power. The two sources agree apart from sandhi (கூடி யெதிர்நிற்கு / மாற்ற லதுவே).

tamil:
மறமானம் மாண்ட வழிச்செலவு தேற்றம்
எனநான்கே ஏமம் படைக்கு.
transliteration:
Maramaanam maanda vazhichchelavu thetram
enanaange emam padaikku.
current_meaning: Bravery, honor, following the good example of earlier soldiers, and being trustworthy are the four things that keep an army safe.
elementary: A good scout troop needs four things: brave members, members who care about doing the right thing, members who follow the good habits of older scouts, and a leader who can trust them. Valluvar says an army needs the same four things to stay safe and strong.
university: The couplet names four qualities: maṟam (மறம், valour), māṉam (மானம், honour, sense of shame at disgrace), māṇṭa vaḻiccelavu (மாண்ட வழிச்செலவு, walking the excellent path of predecessors), and tēṟṟam (தேற்றம்). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take tēṟṟam as ‘being trusted (tested and found reliable) by the king’, while Sivayogi Sivakumar renders it as ‘clear resolve’, a genuine interpretive divergence. Ēmam (ஏமம்) means ‘protection, safeguard’, and the emphatic nāṉkē (‘these four alone’) makes the list exclusive. Both sources agree on the wording (சந்தி: தேற்ற / மெனநான்கே யேமம்).

tamil:
தார்தாங்கிச் செல்வது தானை தலைவந்த
போர்தாங்கும் தன்மை அறிந்து.
transliteration:
Thaarthaangich chelvadhu thaanai thalaivandha
poarthaangum thanmai arindhu.
current_meaning: A true army knows how to stop an attack, and it moves forward by pushing back the front line of the enemy.
elementary: In a game of tug-of-war, the strongest kids stand at the front where the pull is hardest, and they know how to dig their heels in. Valluvar says a good army is like that: it knows how to take the first hard push and keep moving forward.
university: Tār (தார்) is the vanguard, called tūci (தூசி) in the commentaries, which Pope rendered ‘dust-van’ after the dust raised by an advancing force; tāṉai (தானை) is the army. Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as describing an army that, knowing the art of checking an oncoming assault (talaivanta pōr tāṅkum taṉmai), meets and bears the enemy’s vanguard. Solomon Pappaiah reads tār more broadly as the front-line foot soldiers, while Sivayogi Sivakumar takes it as an image of ranks arrayed like a banana bunch, an idiosyncratic reading. Both texts agree (சந்தி: போர்தாங்குந் தன்மை யறிந்து).

tamil:
அடல்தகையும் ஆற்றலும் இல்லெனினும் தானை
படைத்தகையால் பாடு பெறும்.
transliteration:
Adalthagaiyum aatralum illeninum thaanai
padaiththagaiyaal paadu perum.
current_meaning: Even if an army cannot attack well or hold its ground, it can still win fame by looking strong and well equipped.
elementary: A marching band in smart uniforms, all in step, can make a whole crowd stop and stare, even before it plays a note. Valluvar says an army that is neatly lined up and well equipped can earn respect just by how it looks and moves.
university: Aṭaltakai (அடல்தகை) is the capacity to attack and destroy, āṟṟal (ஆற்றல்) the capacity to withstand; paṭaittakai (படைத்தகை) is the excellence of the army’s equipment and array, and pāṭu (பாடு) means ‘renown, dignity’. Parimelazhagar understands the couplet as saying that order and splendour alone can deter or impress an enemy, and Solomon Pappaiah stresses the disciplined beauty of its formation. Kalaignar reads it slightly differently, as saying the array should be even more excellent than attack and defence. The two sources agree (சந்தி: அடல்தகையு மாற்றலு மில்லெனினுந் தானை).

tamil:
சிறுமையும் செல்லாத் துனியும் வறுமையும்
இல்லாயின் வெல்லும் படை.
transliteration:
Sirumaiyum sellaath thuniyum varumaiyum
illaayin vellum padai.
current_meaning: An army will win if its numbers are not shrinking, its soldiers are not always unhappy, and it is not short of supplies.
elementary: A team does best when nobody keeps quitting, nobody is sulking and angry at the coach, and everyone has enough food and kit. Valluvar says an army is the same: keep it whole, happy and well supplied, and it will win.
university: Three defects are named: ciṟumai (சிறுமை, diminution, a shrinking of numbers or strength), cellāt tuṉi (செல்லாத் துனி, a resentment that will not go away, which Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar direct specifically against the king or commander), and vaṟumai (வறுமை, poverty, i.e. unpaid or ill-supplied troops). Solomon Pappaiah follows this reading, while Sivayogi Sivakumar renders ciṟumai as ‘confusion’, a looser gloss. The couplet’s realism about morale and pay matches Kautilya’s detailed discussion of an army’s ‘calamities’. Both sources agree (சந்தி: சிறுமையுஞ் ... வறுமையு / மில்லாயின்).

tamil:
நிலைமக்கள் சால உடைத்தெனினும் தானை
தலைமக்கள் இல்வழி இல்.
transliteration:
Nilaimakkal saala udaiththeninum thaanai
thalaimakkal ilvazhi il.
current_meaning: Even if an army has many loyal soldiers, it cannot last without good leaders.
elementary: A choir may have lots of good singers, but without a conductor they start and stop at different times and it sounds like a mess. Valluvar says an army is the same: many brave soldiers are not enough without a good leader.
university: Nilaimakkaḷ (நிலைமக்கள்) are ‘steadfast men’, read by Parimelazhagar as long-serving, permanent soldiers, and cāla (சால) means ‘in abundance’; talaimakkaḷ (தலைமக்கள்) are the ‘head-men’, i.e. commanders or generals. The final il vaḻi il (இல்வழி இல்) is a terse play: ‘where they are not, (the army) is not’, which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses as the army having no glory and Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as its not being able to hold its ground. The couplet closes the chapter by turning from the troops to their leadership, preparing for the next chapter, Paṭaiccerukku (படைச்செருக்கு, the martial pride of warriors). Both sources agree (சந்தி: சால வுடைத்தெனினுந் ... தலைமக்க ளில்வழி யில்).

tamil:
என்னைமுன் நில்லன்மின் தெவ்விர் பலரென்னை
முன்நின்று கல்நின் றவர்.
transliteration:
Ennaimun nillanmin thevvir palarennai
Munnindru kalnin Ravar.
current_meaning: A soldier warns the enemy: do not stand against my king. Many who once stood before him are now only stones that mark where they died.
elementary: Imagine a champion team whose fans warn the visitors: “Lots of teams came here thinking they would win, and now their names are just on the list of teams we beat.” The warrior is proud of his leader in the same way, and the proud words themselves are meant to make the other side think twice.
university: The chapter title padaiccherukku joins padai (army) and serukku (pride, exultant spirit), and this opening couplet is cast as a battlefield vaunt addressed to thevvir (“you enemies”). Parimelazhagar takes ennai not as “me” but as en + ai, “my lord” (ai = master, chief), so the soldier boasts of his commander rather than of himself; some modern renderings (e.g., Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh.com) read it as the speaker’s own challenge. The punning repetition of nil- / nin- turns on “standing”: those who stood (nindru) against the lord now stand as kal (stone), alluding to the nadukal, the hero-stone erected for fallen warriors, a custom described in the Tolkappiyam’s Purattinai and attested in Sangam puram poetry. Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give the couplet identically; the sandhi split “கல்நின் றவர்” = kal ninravar.

tamil:
கான முயலெய்த அம்பினில் யானை
பிழைத்தவேல் ஏந்தல் இனிது.
transliteration:
Kaana muyaleydha ambinil yaanai
Pizhaiththavel endhal inidhu.
current_meaning: It is better to hold a spear that missed an elephant than an arrow that killed a rabbit in the forest.
elementary: Would you rather say you beat a little kid at chess, or that you lost a close game to the school champion? Trying something truly hard, even if you miss, is more honourable than an easy win over someone weak.
university: The couplet contrasts kaana muyal (the hare of the forest, a small and timid quarry) with yaanai (the elephant, the most formidable target of ancient Tamil warfare), and the arrow (ambu) that succeeded against the hare with the spear (vel) that failed against the elephant (pizhaiththa vel). The key verb endhal, “to hold, to bear,” makes the line about what a warrior is proud to carry: honour belongs to the scale of the attempt, not merely its outcome. Parimelazhagar reads the hare and elephant as figures for weak and mighty enemies, so the teaching concerns the choice of a worthy adversary. Kalaignar’s modern gloss states the point directly: aiming at the strong and missing outranks aiming at the weak and hitting. Both base texts agree on the wording; the sandhi form முயலெய்த = muyal eydha.

tamil:
பேராண்மை என்ப தறுகண்ஒன் றுற்றக்கால்
ஊராண்மை மற்றதன் எஃகு.
transliteration:
Peraanmai enba tharukan ondru utrakkaal
Ooraanmai matradhan eqku.
current_meaning: Having no fear in battle is called great bravery. But helping your enemy when he is in trouble is the sharpest edge of that bravery.
elementary: A good football player plays hard to win. But if a player on the other team falls and gets hurt, the best player stops and helps him up. Being brave is good; being brave and kind is even better.
university: This is the moral centre of the chapter: tharukan (fierceness, unflinching daring) is what people call peraanmai (great manliness or valour), but ooraanmai, helping or showing grace when ondru utrakkaal (“a calamity befalls,” understood as befalling the foe), is its eqku, the keen cutting edge. Parimelazhagar glosses ooraanmai as upakaram (benevolent aid) and the traditional reading takes the misfortune as the enemy’s, so magnanimity to a fallen foe is the sharpest point of heroism. Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar both read it this way; Sivayogi Sivakumar paraphrases more broadly as relieving others’ suffering, even enemies’. The metaphor of eqku (steel, blade-edge) is apt: valour without mercy is a blunt weapon.

tamil:
கைவேல் களிற்றொடு போக்கி வருபவன்
மெய்வேல் பறியா நகும்.
transliteration:
Kaivel kalitrodu pokki varubavan
Meyvel pariyaa nagum.
current_meaning: A hero throws his only spear at an elephant and looks for another weapon. He finds one stuck in his own body, pulls it out, and smiles.
elementary: A firefighter who has used up all the water in one hose doesn’t give up; he grabs whatever is at hand and keeps going, even laughing at how tough the day is. The warrior in this verse is like that: nothing stops him.
university: Kaivel (the spear in hand) is sent off (pokki) with the kalitru (bull elephant), and the warrior, returning weaponless (varubavan), finds a meyvel, an enemy spear stuck in his own body (mey), which he plucks out (pariyaa) and laughs (nagum). Parimelazhagar and later commentators read the laughter as joy at having found a new weapon, not as indifference to pain, so the image is about undiminished fighting spirit. Solomon Pappaiah adds that he takes the spear to hurl at the next elephant. The couplet belongs to the Sangam puram tradition of the hero who welcomes wounds, and its hyperbole should be read as a literary ideal of morale, not a literal description. The two base texts agree verbatim.

tamil:
விழித்தகண் வேல்கொண டெறிய அழித்திமைப்பின்
ஒட்டன்றோ வன்க ணவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Vizhiththakan velkonda eriya azhiththimaippin
Ottandro vankanavarkku.
current_meaning: For truly brave soldiers, even blinking when the enemy’s spear comes at their angry eyes counts as running away.
elementary: A goalkeeper facing a penalty kick tries hard not to flinch, because flinching means he can’t see the ball. The verse says a brave person keeps their eyes open and steady even when something scary is coming right at them.
university: Vizhiththa kan, the wide-open, glaring eye fixed on the foe, is set against azhiththu imaippin, “if it gives way and blinks,” when the enemy hurls (eriya) his spear (vel). For the vankanavar (the hard-eyed, stout-hearted), such a blink is ottu, which commentators gloss as tantamount to puRangodai, turning one’s back in flight; Kalaignar makes this equation explicit. The couplet sets an almost impossible standard to show that heroism is first an inner state: the smallest outward sign of fear already counts as defeat. The sandhi forms கொண டெறிய = kondu eriya and வன்க ணவர்க்கு = vankanavarkku; both base sources agree.

tamil:
விழுப்புண் படாதநாள் எல்லாம் வழுக்கினுள்
வைக்கும்தன் நாளை எடுத்து.
transliteration:
Vizhuppun padaadhanaal ellaam vazhukkinul
Vaikkumdhan naalai eduththu.
current_meaning: A hero counts his days and calls every day wasted on which he did not get a wound in an honorable fight.
elementary: Some athletes feel a day without practice is a day wasted. The warrior here feels that way about days when he did not stand up bravely for his people. The real lesson is about not letting days slip by without doing something that matters.
university: Vizhuppun is a technical term of puram ethics: a wound of honour, received on the chest or face while facing the enemy, as opposed to a wound in the back (a sign of flight). The warrior “takes up” (eduththu) his days and places (vaikkum) every day without such a wound among vazhukku, lapses or wasted days. Solomon Pappaiah explicitly specifies wounds on face and chest, following the traditional reading. The idea echoes Purananuru poems in which a mother checks that her son’s wounds are on his chest. Modern readers may take the hyperbole as a vivid figure for a life measured by service and risk rather than comfort.

tamil:
சுழலும் இசைவேண்டி வேண்டா உயிரார்
கழல்யாப்புக் காரிகை நீர்த்து.
transliteration:
Suzhalum isaivendi vendaa uyiraar
Kazhalyaappuk kaarigai neerththu.
current_meaning: For people who want fame that spreads across the world and do not worry about their own lives, wearing the warrior’s ankle ring is a true decoration.
elementary: A medal looks most beautiful on someone who earned it by being brave for others. The warrior’s anklet in this verse is like that medal: it is beautiful because of the courage of the one who wears it.
university: Suzhalum isai is fame that “circles” or spreads around the world; vendaa uyiraar are those who do not desire (cling to) life; kazhal yaappu is the tying on of the kazhal, the heroic anklet worn by warriors in Tamil tradition; and kaarigai neerththu means it has the nature of a true ornament. The point is that the badge of valour is fitting only on those whose courage is real: on others it would be mere decoration. Solomon Pappaiah glosses isai as the fame that stays on earth after death, unlike the hero who departs. Both base texts agree on the wording; the sandhi யாப்புக் = yaappu + k.

tamil:
உறின்உயிர் அஞ்சா மறவர் இறைவன்
செறினும் சீர்குன்றல் இலர்.
transliteration:
Urin uyir anjaa maravar iraivan
Serinum seerkundral ilar.
current_meaning: Soldiers who do not fear for their lives when war comes do not lose their eagerness to fight, even if the king angrily stops them.
elementary: A team captain may tell an eager player to sit out this game. A truly dedicated player doesn’t sulk or lose heart; they stay ready and keen. The verse says the best soldiers keep their spirit high even when told to wait.
university: Urin (“if it comes,” i.e., if battle arises) uyir anjaa maravar (warriors who do not fear for life) remain seer kundral ilar (without loss of excellence or ardour) even if iraivan serinum, “the king is angry,” which the traditional commentary reads as the king forbidding them to fight. Maravar derives from maram, martial valour, and is the classic Tamil term for the warrior class. Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan read it as the king restraining them; Kalaignar reads it as the king’s displeasure not diminishing their sense of duty. The couplet thus praises discipline without loss of spirit: zeal survives even the leader’s rebuke.

tamil:
இழைத்தது இகவாமைச் சாவாரை யாரே
பிழைத்தது ஒறுக்கிற் பவர்.
transliteration:
Izhaiththadhu igavaamaich chaavaarai yaare
Pizhaiththadhu orukkir pavar.
current_meaning: Who could blame for failure those who die keeping the promise they made?
elementary: If a friend promised to protect you and gave everything trying, no one would say they failed. Keeping your word with all your heart is what counts, even if things don’t turn out perfectly.
university: Izhaiththadhu refers to what one has pledged, the sool or battle-vow sworn before the king; igavaamai is “not transgressing” it; saavaarai are those who die so. The rhetorical question yaare ... orukkirpavar asks “who would punish (or reproach) them” for pizhaiththadhu, the failure. Commentators divide: Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it as those who die fighting in fulfilment of their vow, whom no one can reproach; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as even if the vow went unfulfilled, death in the attempt removes all blame. Either way, death in fidelity to one’s word places the warrior beyond censure.

tamil:
புரந்தார்கண் நீர்மல்கச் சாகிற்பின் சாக்காடு
இரந்துகோள் தக்கது உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Purandhaarkan neermalgach chaagirpin saakkaadu
Irandhukol thakkadhu udaiththu.
current_meaning: If a soldier can die in a way that brings tears to the eyes of the king who cared for him, that death is worth begging for.
elementary: When someone gives everything to protect others, the people who loved and led them are deeply moved and never forget them. The verse says the greatest honour is to be so loyal and good that your leader is moved to tears for you.
university: Purandhaar are “those who nurtured or protected” the warrior, chiefly the king who maintained him; the condition is that their kan (eyes) neer malga, brim with tears; such a saakkaadu (death) has a worth that makes it irandhu kol thakkadhu, fit to be obtained even by begging (iravu, the act the Kural elsewhere treats as shameful). The paradox is deliberate: Valluvar, who devotes chapters 106-107 to the shame of begging, says this one thing is worth begging for. The couplet closes the chapter on the bond between ruler and soldier rather than on slaughter: the measure of the death is the grief of the one who knew its worth. Solomon Pappaiah renders the king’s eyes as those that weigh the heroes’ deeds; the other commentators take the tears literally.

tamil:
செயற்கரிய யாவுள நட்பின் அதுபோல்
வினைக்கரிய யாவுள காப்பு.
transliteration:
Seyarkariya yaavula natpin adhupol
vinaikkariya yaavula kaappu.
current_meaning: What is as hard to gain as friendship? And once you have it, what protection is as hard for any enemy to break?
elementary: Making a real friend is like growing a tree from a seed: it takes a long time and lots of care. But once the tree is big, it gives you shade that no storm can easily take away. A true friend is both the hardest thing to grow and the best shelter to have.
university: The chapter opens the Natpiyal (நட்பியல், section on friendship, chapters 79-95) of the Porutpal, where friendship is treated not only as a private good but as one of the supports of a king and of any householder. The couplet is built on two parallel rhetorical questions: seyaRku ariya (செயற்கரிய, hard to make or acquire) and vinaikku ariya kaappu (வினைக்கரிய காப்பு, a guard hard for hostile action to breach). Parimelazhagar reads the second line as ‘what guard is so hard for enemies’ efforts to overcome’, which is why Pope renders it ‘What so sure defence ’gainst all that foe can do?’; Mu. Varadarasanar instead takes vinai as one’s own undertakings, so that friendship is the rare protection for one’s work, and Solomon Pappaiah combines the two senses. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நிறைநீர நீரவர் கேண்மை பிறைமதிப்
பின்னீர பேதையார் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Niraineera neeravar kenmai piraimadhip
pinneera pedhaiyaar natpu.
current_meaning: Friendship with good people grows like the moon getting bigger each night. Friendship with fools shrinks like the moon after it is full.
elementary: Think of the moon. Some nights it starts as a thin smile and gets bigger and brighter every night. Other times it starts big and round and shrinks a little every night. Good friends are like the growing moon: each week you know them, the friendship gets fuller. Silly friends are like the shrinking moon: exciting at first, then less and less.
university: The couplet is one of the Kural’s best-known lunar similes. Niraineera (நிறைநீர) means ‘of the nature of filling up’, that is, the waxing crescent (piRai, பிறை) that grows to fullness; piRaimadhip pinneera (பிறைமதிப் பின்னீர) means ‘of the nature of the moon after fullness’, the waning phase. Neeravar (நீரவர்) are ‘people of good nature’ (from நீர்மை, quality), and Parimelazhagar glosses them as the wise and good, set against pēdhaiyār (பேதையார், fools). Kēṇmai and natpu are near-synonyms for friendship, used for variety. Parimelazhagar notes that the first kind of friendship starts small and grows by the day, while the second starts at its fullest and then declines. The text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நவில்தொறும் நூல்நயம் போலும் பயில்தொறும்
பண்புடை யாளர் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Navildhorum noolnayam polum payildhorum
panpudai yaalar thodarpu.
current_meaning: Friendship with good people is like a great book. The more often you go back to it, the more you enjoy it.
elementary: Do you have a favourite book you have read many times? Each time, you notice something new and like it even more. Being friends with a kind, good person is like that book: every time you spend time together, the friendship gets sweeter.
university: The couplet sets two verbs of repetition side by side: navil-thoRum (நவில்தொறும், ‘each time it is studied or recited’) and payil-thoRum (பயில்தொறும், ‘each time one associates’). Nūl-nayam (நூல்நயம்) is the excellence or beauty of a learned text, which reveals new depths with every reading; paṇbudaiyāḷar (பண்புடையாளர்) are people of refined character, and thodarpu (தொடர்பு) is their companionship. Parimelazhagar’s point is that good company, unlike pleasures that tire with use, grows sweeter with each meeting, just as a good book does. The comparison fits the Kural’s own high regard for study (chapters 40-42). ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give the same text; பண்புடை யாளர் is a metrical split of பண்புடையாளர்.

tamil:
நகுதற் பொருட்டன்று நட்டல் மிகுதிக்கண்
மேற்சென்று இடித்தற் பொருட்டு.
transliteration:
Nagudhar poruttandru nattal migudhikkan
merchendru idiththar poruttu.
current_meaning: We make friends not just to laugh together, but so that when a friend goes the wrong way, we can step in first and correct them.
elementary: Imagine your friend is about to cross the road without looking. A pretend friend just keeps laughing with them. A real friend grabs their arm and says, ‘Stop! That’s dangerous!’ even if it makes them a bit cross. Friends are for fun, but most of all they are for stopping each other from doing something wrong.
university: This is the chapter’s key statement on the moral purpose of friendship. Nagudhal (நகுதல்) is laughing or merriment; nattal (நட்டல்) is the act of befriending; migudhi (மிகுதி) means excess, that is, a friend’s overstepping or wrongdoing; mēRsenRu (மேற்சென்று) means ‘going ahead, taking the initiative’; and iditthal (இடித்தல், literally ‘striking’) is the classical term for sharp rebuke, related to iḍipparai (இடிப்பார், the rebuking counsellor) in kural 448. Parimelazhagar stresses that the friend must rebuke before the fault grows, without waiting to be asked. Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print மேற்செனறு, which looks like a shared typing error; the standard reading மேற்சென்று (as in Mu. Varadarasanar’s ‘முற்பட்டுச் சென்று’ gloss) is given here.

tamil:
புணர்ச்சி பழகுதல் வேண்டா உணர்ச்சிதான்
நட்பாங் கிழமை தரும்.
transliteration:
Punarchchi pazhagudhal vendaa unarchchidhaan
natpaang kizhamai tharum.
current_meaning: Friendship does not need you to meet often or know each other for long. Thinking and feeling alike is enough to make true friends.
elementary: Sometimes you meet a pen pal or a cousin who lives far away, and even though you rarely see each other, you just ‘get’ each other. You like the same things and feel the same way. Valluvar says that feeling of understanding is what really makes a friend, not how many times you hang out.
university: PuNarchchi (புணர்ச்சி) here means being together or meeting, and pazhaguthal (பழகுதல்) long familiarity; both are declared unnecessary (vēṇdā). What creates friendship is uNarchchi (உணர்ச்சி), which Parimelazhagar glosses as like-mindedness, a mutual understanding of each other’s feelings; this alone gives natpu-ām kizhamai (நட்பாங் கிழமை), the intimate right or claim that belongs to friendship. Commentators traditionally cite the Sangam friendship of the Chola king Kōpperuñcōḻaṉ and the poet Pisirāndaiyār, who were said to have loved each other for years without meeting, and of whom the poet joined the king in his ritual fast unto death (Puranaṉūru 215-217). The text is the same on both web sources.

tamil:
முகநக நட்பது நட்பன்று நெஞ்சத்து
அகநக நட்பது நட்பு.
transliteration:
Muganaga natpadhu natpandru nenjaththu
aganaga natpadhu natpu.
current_meaning: Friendship that only makes the face smile is not real friendship. Real friendship makes the heart smile inside.
elementary: Some people smile at you only on the outside, like a mask, but inside they don’t really care. A true friend is happy all the way inside when they see you, even if they don’t make a big show of it. Real friendship is a smile in the heart, not just on the face.
university: The couplet turns on a pair of near-rhyming compounds: muga-naga (முகநக, ‘so that the face smiles’) and aga-naga (அகநக, ‘so that the inside smiles’), with nenjatthu (நெஞ்சத்து, ‘in the heart’) making the inner sense explicit. Naga (நக) means to laugh, smile or blossom, so both commentators and translators often render it as the face or heart ‘blooming’. Parimelazhagar takes the first kind of friendship to be outward courtesy only, and the second to be friendship rooted in love (anbu). The word natpu appears four times in seven words, which gives the verse its proverbial ring. The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அழிவி னவைநீக்கி ஆறுய்த்து அழிவின்கண்
அல்லல் உழப்பதாம் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Azhivi navainikki aaruyththu azhivinkan
allal uzhappadhaam natpu.
current_meaning: A friend stops you from doing what would ruin you, guides you onto the right path, and shares your pain when trouble comes anyway.
elementary: A real friend does three things. First, if you’re about to do something that will get you into big trouble, they stop you. Second, they help you find a better thing to do. Third, if something bad happens anyway, they don’t run away; they stay and feel sad with you. That’s what a friend is for.
