university: The verse lists three duties in order: azhivinavai nīkki (அழிவினவை நீக்கி, ‘removing the things that lead to ruin’), āRu uytthu (ஆறுய்த்து, ‘sending him along the right way’, from āRu, path), and, if ruin still comes (azhivinkaN, அழிவின்கண்), allal uzhappathu (அல்லல் உழப்பது, ‘toiling in his distress alongside him’). Parimelazhagar takes the first two as prevention and correction, carrying on from the rebuke of kural 784, and the third as the friend’s readiness to share in misfortune he could not prevent. The printed line அழிவி னவைநீக்கி is a metrical split of அழிவினவை நீக்கி. Both web sources give the same text, and Pope’s ‘it weeps with him who weeps’ echoes Romans 12:15.

tamil:
உடுக்கை இழந்தவன் கைபோல ஆங்கே
இடுக்கண் களைவதாம் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Udukkai izhandhavan kaipola aange
idukkan kalaivadhaam natpu.
current_meaning: When a person’s clothes slip, the hand rushes to catch them. In the same way, a true friend rushes right away to end a friend’s trouble.
elementary: If your trousers started slipping in front of the whole class, your hand would grab them right away. You wouldn’t stop to think or wait to be asked; your hand just does it. A true friend helps you in trouble that fast and that naturally, as if they were your own hand.
university: This is one of the most quoted images in the Kural. Udukkai (உடுக்கை) is a garment and izhandhavan (இழந்தவன்) the one losing it, so the picture is of clothing slipping, which Solomon Pappaiah and others place ‘in front of many people’ (பலர் முன்னே) to bring out the urgency of shame. The key word is āngē (ஆங்கே, ‘there and then, at once’): the hand acts by reflex, without being asked and without thinking. Parimelazhagar notes that the hand acts before the mind decides, and so friendship should remove idukkaN (இடுக்கண், distress) before the friend has to ask. The image also implies that a friend is part of one’s own body. Both web sources give the same text.

tamil:
நட்பிற்கு வீற்றிருக்கை யாதெனின் கொட்பின்றி
ஒல்லும்வாய் ஊன்றும் நிலை.
transliteration:
Natpirku veetrirukkai yaadhenin kotpindri
ollumvaai oondrum nilai.
current_meaning: Where does friendship sit like a king on a throne? In always being ready to hold up a friend in every way you can.
elementary: Think of a walking stick that an old person leans on. It doesn’t move around or give up; it’s always there to take their weight. Valluvar says the very best friendship is like that stick: steady, never changing its mind, and always ready to hold you up however it can.
university: VīRRirukkai (வீற்றிருக்கை) means a throne or seat of majesty, so the question is ‘where is friendship’s throne?’, that is, what is its highest state. The answer has three parts: kotpu inRi (கொட்பின்றி, ‘without kotpu’, a word meaning whirling or wavering, so ‘without change of heart’); ollum vāy (ஒல்லும்வாய், ‘wherever and however possible’); and ūnRum nilai (ஊன்றும் நிலை, ‘the state of propping up, supporting’, as a staff supports). Parimelazhagar explains ollumvāy as helping in every way available toward the friend’s virtue and wealth, and kotpinri as never wavering in mind, whatever the times. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah gloss kotpinri as ‘always, without change’. Both web sources give the same text.

tamil:
இனையர் இவரெமக்கு இன்னம்யாம் என்று
புனையினும் புல்லென்னும் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Inaiyar ivaremakku innamyaam endru
punaiyinum pullennum natpu.
current_meaning: When friends go around saying, “He means this much to me, and I mean that much to him,” the friendship becomes cheap, however nicely they praise it.
elementary: Imagine two kids who keep telling everyone, ‘I’m her best friend, and I gave her THREE presents, and she’s SO lucky to have me!’ It starts to sound like showing off, and the friendship feels less special. Real friends don’t keep score or brag about it; they just are friends.
university: Inaiyar (இனையர்) means ‘such-and-such persons’ and innam (இன்னம்) ‘such-and-such’; the friend who says ‘he is so much to us, we are so much to him’ is measuring and advertising the friendship. Punaiyinum (புனையினும், ‘even if one adorns or praises it’) and pullennum (புல்லென்னும், ‘it looks mean or paltry’, from pul, grass, a common figure for worthlessness) complete the thought. Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as a warning that true friends do not set their mutual services side by side or display their closeness, because keeping such accounts belongs to traders, not friends. The chapter thus ends where it began, by setting real friendship above any outward show. Both web sources give the same text; இவரெமக்கு is இவர் எமக்கு joined by sandhi.

tamil:
நாடாது நட்டலிற் கேடில்லை நட்டபின்
வீடில்லை நட்பாள் பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Naadaadhu nattalir kedillai nattapin
veedillai natpaal bavarkku.
current_meaning: Nothing is more harmful than making friends without first checking a person carefully. For loyal people, once a friendship is made, they cannot walk away from it.
elementary: Imagine tying your shoelace to a friend’s shoelace for a three-legged race. Once the knot is tight, you have to run together wherever the other person goes. So before you tie the knot, make sure your partner is someone who runs the right way.
university: The chapter opens on a paradox: the very loyalty that makes a person a good friend is what makes a careless friendship dangerous. Natpaalbavar (நட்பாள்பவர்) are ‘those who maintain friendship’, people for whom a friend once made cannot be dropped; veedu (வீடு) here means ‘release’ or ‘leaving off’, not ‘house’. Parimelazhagar draws the inference the couplet implies: since the good never abandon a friend, there is no evil equal to friendship formed without naadal (நாடல், inquiry), and so the examination must come before, not after. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it the same way, while Kalaignar paraphrases it as ‘a bad friendship taken up without inquiry brings harm one cannot escape’. The text is the same in ytamizh, thirukkural.net and the sandhi-joined edition at thirukkural-thamizh.org.

tamil:
ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து கொள்ளாதான் கேண்மை கடைமுறை
தான்சாம் துயரம் தரும்.
transliteration:
Aaindhaaindhu kollaadhaan kenmai kadaimurai
thaansaam thuyaram tharum.
current_meaning: If you make a friend without checking that person again and again, the friendship will bring you pain so bitter it could kill you in the end.
elementary: If you eat a mushroom from the woods without checking it, it might look fine today and make you very sick tomorrow. Friends are like that too. Look carefully, and then look again, before you let someone become your close friend.
university: The doubling aaindhu-aaindhu (ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து, ‘having examined and examined’) insists that a single check is not enough; Parimelazhagar understands it as examining a person by many means and on many occasions. Kenmai (கேண்மை) is intimate friendship, and kadaimurai (கடைமுறை) means ‘at the last’ or ‘in the final course’, so the harm is delayed, which is why it is so easily ignored. Thaan saam thuyaram (தான்சாம் துயரம்) is ‘a sorrow from which he himself dies’; most modern commentators, including Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar, take this as hyperbole for grief that can bring a person to death. The sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh.org reads தான்சாந் துயரந் தரும், a purely orthographic difference from the ytamizh and thirukkural.net texts.

tamil:
குணமும் குடிமையும் குற்றமும் குன்றா
இனனும் அறிந்தியாக்க நட்பு.
transliteration:
Gunamum kudimaiyum kutramum kundraa
inanum arindhiyaakka natpu.
current_meaning: Make someone your friend only after you know their character, their family, their faults, and the people they spend time with.
elementary: Before you join a new team, you watch how the players behave, who their coach is, what mistakes they make, and who they hang out with. Valluvar says to do the same four checks before you choose a close friend.
university: This couplet supplies the checklist for the chapter’s ‘investigation’: gunam (குணம், disposition or character), kudimai (குடிமை, lineage, the family in which one is raised), kutram (குற்றம், faults), and kundraa inam (குன்றா இனம், one’s abiding associates or kin). Parimelazhagar takes inam as the circle of relatives and companions who stand by a person, on the principle, developed in chapter 46 (Sitrinam Seraamai), that a person takes on the quality of the company he keeps; Puliyur Kesigan accordingly glosses it as ‘the companions who stay with him’. Arindhu yaakka (அறிந்து யாக்க) means ‘form it having known’. The ytamizh and thirukkural.net texts read குணமும், while the sandhi-joined edition reads குணனுங் குடிமையுங், an older spelling with the same meaning.

tamil:
குடிப்பிறந்து தன்கண் பழிநாணு வானைக்
கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Kudippirandhu thankan pazhinaanu vaanaik
koduththum kolalvendum natpu.
current_meaning: Make friends with someone from a good family who feels ashamed of doing wrong, even if it costs you something.
elementary: Some friends are like a good umbrella: worth saving your pocket money for. A friend who comes from a caring home and feels bad if he does something wrong is that kind of friend, so it is worth giving up something to have him.
university: Kudippirandhu (குடிப்பிறந்து) means ‘born into a good family’, the kudi of chapter 96 (Kudimai), and pazhi naanuvaan (பழிநாணுவான்) is ‘one who feels shame at blame’, that is, someone whose sense of honour keeps him from disgraceful acts. Koduththum (கொடுத்தும், ‘even by giving’) carries the force of ‘even at a price’. Parimelazhagar takes it literally as giving wealth to secure such a friend, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah likewise say ‘even by paying a price’, while Kalaignar softens it to ‘by any means’. After three couplets of warning, the chapter turns here to the positive: some friendships are worth paying for. The ytamizh and thirukkural.net texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition reads தன்கட் and கொடுத்துங் … வேண்டு, orthographic variants only.

tamil:
அழச்சொல்லி அல்லது இடித்து வழக்கறிய
வல்லார்நட்பு ஆய்ந்து கொளல்.
transliteration:
Azhachcholli alladhu idiththu vazhakkariya
vallaarnatpu aaindhu kolal.
current_meaning: Find and keep friends who can make you cry with hard truths, scold you sharply when you are wrong, and understand how the world works.
elementary: A good coach sometimes tells you, ‘That was wrong, do it again,’ and it can make you want to cry. But that coach makes you better. Valluvar says to choose friends like that coach, not friends who only say nice things.
university: Azhach cholli (அழச்சொல்லி) is ‘speaking so as to make one weep’ and idiththu (இடித்து) is ‘striking’, that is, rebuking hard; the same verb appears in kural 448 of the idikkum thunai, the counsellor who rebukes a king. Parimelazhagar distinguishes the two: the friend makes you weep with counsel before a wrong is done, and rebukes you sharply after it is done; Solomon Pappaiah follows this two-step reading. Vazhakku ariya valla (வழக்கறிய வல்ல) means ‘able to make one know the ways of the world’, adding practical wisdom to frankness. Both ytamizh and thirukkural.net print வல்லார்நடபு, which is missing its pulli; the sandhi-joined edition’s வல்லார்நட் பாய்ந்து confirms the reading வல்லார்நட்பு used here.

tamil:
கேட்டினும் உண்டோர் உறுதி கிளைஞரை
நீட்டி அளப்பதோர் கோல்.
transliteration:
Kettinum undor urudhi kilaignarai
neetti alappadhor kol.
current_meaning: Even bad times have one good side. They are a ruler that measures how far your friends and relatives will really go for you.
elementary: When it rains, you find out which umbrellas have holes. When something bad happens to you, you find out which friends stay. That is the one good thing about a bad day: it shows you who your real friends are.
university: Kedu (கேடு) is ruin or misfortune and urudhi (உறுதி) is ‘benefit’ or ‘firm good’; the -um in kettinum gives ‘even in ruin’. Kilaignar (கிளைஞர்) literally means kin, ‘those of the same branch’, but Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators extend it to friends, since the chapter is about friendship. The image of neetti alappadhu oor kol (நீட்டி அளப்பதோர் கோல், ‘a rod that measures by stretching out’) is a surveyor’s measuring rod laid end to end, which measures exactly how far each person’s affection reaches. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both stress the paradox that harm itself becomes the instrument of knowledge. The sandhi-joined text reads கேட்டினு முண்டோ ருறுதி, the same words.

tamil:
ஊதியம் என்பது ஒருவற்குப் பேதையார்
கேண்மை ஒரீஇ விடல்.
transliteration:
Oodhiyam enbadhu oruvarkup pedhaiyaar
kenmai oreei vidal.
current_meaning: The real gain for a person is to give up friendship with fools completely.
elementary: If your kite is tied to a heavy rock, it can never fly. Cutting the string to the rock is not a loss; it is how the kite goes up. Letting go of a friend who keeps pulling you into silly trouble is the same kind of win.
university: Oodhiyam (ஊதியம்) is ‘profit’ or ‘gain’, a deliberately commercial word in a chapter of the Porutpal. Pedhaiyaar (பேதையார்) are fools in the specific Kural sense defined in chapter 84 (Pedhaimai): people who take up what harms them and drop what helps them. Oreei (ஒரீஇ) is an alapedai (sound-lengthened) form of oruvi, ‘having abandoned’, and with vidal (விடல், ‘letting go’) it makes ‘to abandon and let go entirely’. Parimelazhagar and Puliyur Kesigan read the couplet as applying to a friendship already formed with a fool unknowingly: leaving it as soon as the folly is recognised is itself a gain. The sandhi-joined text reads ஊதிய மென்ப தொருவற்குப் … யொரீஇ, the same words.

tamil:
உள்ளற்க உள்ளம் சிறுகுவ கொள்ளற்க
அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Ullarka ullam sirukuva kollarka
allarkan aatraruppaar natpu.
current_meaning: Do not think about things that make your spirit weak, and do not make friends with people who will leave you when trouble comes.
elementary: Some friends are like a bicycle that only works on sunny days: the moment it rains, the chain falls off. Do not count on a friend like that. Pick friends who will still be pedalling with you when the road gets muddy.
university: The couplet sets two prohibitions side by side. Ullarka ullam siruguva (உள்ளற்க உள்ளம் சிறுகுவ) is ‘do not think the things that make the mind small’; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take this as avoiding whatever saps one’s energy and resolve (ookkam), and Parimelazhagar treats the first line as an analogy for the second: just as one should not entertain spirit-shrinking thoughts, one should not take up such friends. Allarkan aatraruppaar (அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார்) are ‘those who cut off the way in time of distress’, people who withdraw their support exactly when it is needed. Puliyur Kesigan reads the first line differently, as a warning not to think meanly of a friend, which shows the line is open to more than one interpretation. The sandhi-joined text reads உள்ளற்க வுள்ளஞ் … வல்லற்க ணாற்றறுப்பார், the same words.
